Driver Analysis

Nationwide E15/E10 Fuel-Blending Waivers Expanding Ethanol Offtake

On March 25, 2026, the EPA issued its first-ever nationwide emergency fuel waiver permitting E15 (15% ethanol blend) sales year-round across all 50 states at a common 10 psi Reid Vapor Pressure standard, effective May 1-20, 2026, with the agency signaling intent to renew consecutive 20-day waivers to sustain the policy through the summer driving season. This directly expands the addressable throughput for the roughly 91-92% of US corn-based ethanol that runs through dry-mill facilities, as confirmed by USDA grain-crushing data showing dry mills processing between 91.5% and 92.7% of total grain used for fuel ethanol from mid-2025 through mid-2026.

Structurally, this shifts dry-mill economics from a volume-capped model — where plants historically throttled output around the 10% “blend wall” toward a demand-elastic model in which incremental capacity utilization and second-shift running hours become the primary margin lever, rather than new capital expansion.

Growth Energy projects an additional 1,200 E15 retail locations coming online in 2026 alone, on top of roughly 5,000 existing sites, while a parallel legislative push seeks to make the waiver permanent, which would remove the annual regulatory-renewal risk that currently forces ethanol producers to hedge forward contracts conservatively.

Opponents estimate that permanent year-round E15 could drive a roughly 50% expansion in ethanol demand, which — even discounted for advocacy bias — signals a material upside skew to dry-mill utilization rates and corn-draw volumes through 2027-2028.

Drivers Impact Analysis

Restraint Analysis

Feedstock (Corn) Price Volatility Compressing Crush Margins

Corn constitutes roughly 80% of the direct variable cost structure at a dry-mill ethanol facility, and 2025 futures swung from below $4.00 per bushel to nearly $5.00 per bushel within a single crop year, dragging weekly net production profit across a wide band from a loss of $0.05 per gallon to a peak gain of $0.56 per gallon before settling at a full-year average of roughly $0.21 per gallon; this single-input dependency means every $0.25/bushel swing in corn typically moves plant-level operating margin by an estimated $0.02-0.03 per gallon, a magnitude large enough to flip a mid-sized 100-million-gallon-per-year plant between an annualized $2 million profit and a comparable loss position within a single quarter, forcing smaller, non-vertically-integrated operators without forward corn-basis contracts to curtail run-rates, delay maintenance CapEx, and rely on co-product (DDGS, corn oil) revenue as a margin buffer rather than a growth lever.

Restraint Impact Analysis

Opportunity Analysis

45Q Carbon Capture Monetization via CO2 Pipeline Offtake

Unlike the SAF and E15 drivers already embedded in baseline volume forecasts, carbon capture monetization represents an entirely new, non-ethanol revenue line that most dry-mill operators have not yet activated at scale, since the federal 45Q credit — locked at $85 per metric ton for point-source geologic storage under the 2025 reconciliation bill, with inflation indexing beginning in 2027 off a 2025 base year only becomes commercially attractive once a plant secures pipeline access, and Summit Carbon Solutions’ Midwest project, which has grown to include 57 partner ethanol facilities after years of permitting delays, is now targeting operational start in 2026, unlocking an estimated $15-25 million in annual incremental credit revenue for a cluster of mid-sized plants that previously vented fermentation CO2 as a zero-value byproduct; because the qualifying-facility construction deadline was extended to January 1, 2026, plants that have not yet contracted pipeline capacity face a closing strategic window, making this a genuine white-space capital-allocation decision rather than a currently monetized driver, with early movers positioned to convert an emissions liability into a margin-accretive credit stream worth an estimated $0.08-0.12 per gallon once fully scaled.

Opportunity Impact Analysis

Challenges Analysis

Skilled Operator and Maintenance Talent Gap

The structural vulnerability originates in an aging technical workforce compounded by a broader manufacturing recruitment crisis, with 79% of manufacturing leaders citing skilled labor as their top operational challenge entering 2026, a figure up 9 percentage points from the prior year, and this shortage directly hits dry-mill plants that require specialized instrumentation technicians, fermentation biochemists, and boiler-certified operators who cannot be trained on standard community-college timelines shorter than 12-18 months; quantitatively, an estimated 15-20% vacancy rate for skilled maintenance roles at rural Corn Belt facilities forces plants to rely on overtime premiums that can inflate labor cost per gallon by 6-10%, delay preventive-maintenance cycles by an estimated 2-4 weeks per quarter, and constrain the pace at which newly commissioned 45Q or SAF-adjacent retrofit lines can be staffed and ramped to full capacity; the long-term corporate adjustment required is a shift from reactive local hiring toward structured apprenticeship pipelines, cross-training programs, and in some cases remote-monitoring/automation investment to offset headcount gaps, a resolution path that realistically spans four-plus years given training-cycle and workforce-demographic realities.

Challenges Impact Analysis

Geopolitical Impact Analysis

Ongoing Wars Increase Grain and Cost Pressure on Dry Milling

The Russia–Ukraine war and conflict around Middle Eastern shipping routes are keeping the Dry Milling Market exposed to grain, fertilizer, energy, and freight volatility. Ukraine remains an important supplier of corn and other grains, so damage to Black Sea infrastructure, port interruptions, and slower shipments can tighten raw-material availability and raise procurement costs.

The European Commission reported in July 2026 that around 255 million tonnes of Ukrainian grain, oilseeds, and related products had been exported since May 2022 through EU Solidarity Lanes and Ukrainian Black Sea ports, showing how global grain flows still depend on secure transport corridors.

Price pressure has also returned. FAO reported that world maize prices increased 3.6% in July 2026, partly because firmer energy markets and geopolitical tensions affected commodity sentiment. UNCTAD also reported that ship transits through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen by about 95% during the 2026 disruption, lifting oil, gas, freight, marine-fuel, and insurance costs.

Regional Insights

North America dominates the Dry Milling Market with a 40.00% share, valued at around USD 0.80 billion.

North America maintained a dominant position in the Dry Milling Market in 2025, capturing more than a 40.00% share and generating about USD 0.80 billion. The region benefits from a large corn base, mature ethanol infrastructure, established feed demand, and extensive food-processing capacity. USDA data show that North American corn production was estimated at 472.9 million metric tons for 2025/26, while regional corn imports reached 28.95 million metric tons.

The strength of dry milling is particularly visible in the U.S. ethanol industry. USDA reported that dry mills accounted for 92.0% of corn used for fuel-alcohol production in April 2026, when 428 million bushels of corn went into fuel alcohol. Canada further supports regional raw-material availability, producing 14.9 million tonnes of grain corn in 2025. These volumes provide reliable corn supplies for ethanol, DDGS, flour, meal, grits, and other dry-milled products.

Asia Pacific is emerging as the fastest-growing regional opportunity for dry milling, supported by expanding corn output, feed manufacturing, packaged foods, and higher-value grain processing. China provides the clearest industrial base. FAO estimated Chinese maize production at a record 299 million tonnes in 2025, with around 80% of the national crop produced in the North China Plain.

USDA Foreign Agricultural Service reported that China’s corn-processing capacity reached about 130 million metric tons by the end of 2025, with more than 70% of capacity focused on starch-based processing. The sector consumed more than 80 million metric tons of corn in 2025, equal to 26% of total corn use. USDA also projected China’s 2026/27 corn production at 306 million metric tons. This expanding processing base creates opportunities for dry-milled food ingredients, feed products, fermentation inputs, and value-added corn derivatives.

Its Vantage Corn Processors business, which includes corn dry-milling ethanol operations, reported USD 127 million operating profit in Q1 2026 and USD 85 million in Q2 2026.

text:
Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd. has signed a sales agreement with a global energy major to supply an Industrial Continuous Waste Plastic Pyrolysis Production Line, strengthening its position in the rapidly developing waste-to-fuel market. The project will use Niutech’s proprietary continuous pyrolysis technology to process waste plastics into pyrolysis oil, which will then undergo hydrotreatment to produce Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

The production line will be installed at one of the customer’s large-scale refineries and will have a single-unit processing capacity ranging from 10,000 to 50,000 tonnes per year. The agreement represents Niutech’s first entry into the global energy company’s equipment supply chain and provides an important commercial validation of its industrial-scale pyrolysis technology.

SAF has emerged as an important pathway for reducing carbon emissions from the aviation sector. Regulatory support in Europe is also accelerating demand for alternative aviation fuels. Under the European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, airlines are required to use a minimum 2% SAF blend from 2025, with the requirement increasing to 6% by 2030 and eventually reaching 70% by 2050.

While used cooking oil (UCO) remains a key feedstock for SAF production, limited availability could constrain its long-term growth. As a result, waste plastic is gaining attention as an alternative feedstock for producing aviation fuel. Niutech’s technology is designed to convert low-value plastic waste, including polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), polystyrene (PS), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), and nylon, into pyrolysis oil. The technology can process both individual plastic streams and mixed waste plastics.

A key advantage of the system is its ability to process waste plastics without complicated pre-treatment processes such as washing, sorting, and drying. This could help reduce feedstock preparation requirements and improve the commercial viability of large-scale waste plastic recycling and fuel production.

Niutech has already deployed its continuous waste plastic pyrolysis technology commercially in several markets, including the United Kingdom, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand, Vietnam, and China. The company has completed multiple continuous pyrolysis projects with capacities in the 10,000-tpy range.

According to Niutech, large-scale pyrolysis projects require strong continuous operating capabilities and reliable equipment. The company said its nearly four decades of experience in pyrolysis technology and its extensive project portfolio helped demonstrate the maturity of its industrial continuous systems. The latest agreement further strengthens the company’s credentials in large-scale waste-to-fuel applications and could create opportunities for additional refinery-integrated pyrolysis projects.

Impact on Product & Chemical Commodity Prices

The agreement is bullish for waste plastic pyrolysis oil and SAF, as greater commercial deployment could increase demand for waste plastics as feedstock and strengthen the market for recycled hydrocarbon intermediates. Over time, expanded pyrolysis capacity could increase the supply of pyrolysis oil, potentially limiting price gains if production scales rapidly. For PP, PE, PS, ABS, and nylon, increased diversion of post-consumer waste into pyrolysis could reduce the availability of recycled feedstock and support prices for waste plastic streams. However, the impact on virgin polymer prices should remain limited initially. For tracked commodities, the development is likely to create moderate long-term upward support for recycled materials, while adding competitive pressure to conventional fossil-based feedstocks.

Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI) says Airbus is positioning the country as a regional hub for its digital aviation business, with Bangkok set to serve as the headquarters for Airbus’s Skywise unit across Asia.

BOI Secretary-General Narit Therdsteerasukdi said Airbus considers Thailand one of its core business bases after meeting Bert Porteman, president of Airbus Thailand, at the Rasa Tower II office in Bangkok.

Airbus has established a regional Flight Operations Center of Excellence under the Skywise brand, its digital arm, which will support the development of digital and modern aviation technology across Asia.

Airbus currently employs more than 200 people in Thailand, more than triple its 2022 headcount, with 85% being Thai nationals across engineering, software, design and technical roles. The company plans to hire more than 40 additional staff this year.

The BOI and Airbus also discussed building on Thailand’s automotive parts sector to enter the aircraft components supply chain, training personnel for maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work, and developing Thailand as a production base for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Airbus, Europe’s largest aircraft and defence systems manufacturer, has operated in Thailand for more than 40 years and has over 150 commercial aircraft in the country, with customers including Thai Airways, Bangkok Airways, Thai AirAsia and Thai Vietjet.

It also collaborates with GISTDA on the THEOS satellite programme, with Thai Aviation Industries (TAI) on military aircraft maintenance, and with the CP Group on sustainable aviation fuel.

Deepening ties

A key focus of the meeting was expanding Skywise, which develops airline software covering flight data analysis, safety management, crew planning and predictive maintenance. Airbus is expanding its Skywise software testing team in Thailand, using the country as its sole global testing base before software is delivered to airline customers.

Narit said Airbus intends to make Bangkok its Skywise headquarters for Asia, covering ASEAN, China, India, Japan and South Korea, reflecting Thailand’s readiness to support advanced engineering and software work with highly skilled personnel.

Airbus executives estimate global passenger numbers and fleet sizes will double over the next 20 years, driving demand for more than 20,000 new aircraft, against a current backlog of more than 9,000 aircraft on order. However, supply chain issues, labour shortages and geopolitical tensions are pushing manufacturers to diversify their supply chains.

Airbus views Thailand’s geopolitical neutrality and skilled workforce as strengths that could expand its role from automotive parts and precision components into aircraft structures, composite materials and cabin interiors. Airbus currently has about 80 Tier 1 to Tier 3 suppliers in Thailand.

A pathway for young minds

On workforce development, Airbus partners with King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang, Kasetsart University and Chulalongkorn University on aerospace engineering courses, alongside training in digital technology and AI.

For MRO, Airbus works with Thai Aviation Industries on helicopter and military aircraft maintenance, though a large-scale commercial MRO centre remains constrained by a shortage of technicians.

Airbus said Thailand has potential to become a leading SAF producer given its agricultural waste and ethanol industry, starting with used cooking oil in the short term and progressing to ethanol-based and synthetic fuels over the longer term, though this would require significant investment and coordination between government, industry and airlines.

Narit said the discussions reflect an opportunity for Thailand to raise its role across the aviation industry, from digital work to supply chains, MRO and fuel production, and that the BOI is ready to coordinate with Airbus and relevant agencies to advance the sector further.

text:
Business Leadership South Africa (BLSA) and Eskom, which have recently expressed public disagreement over the nature of the unbundling of the State-owned utility, have issued a joint statement in support of creating a Transmission System Operator (TSO) with the grid assets, while committing to engage over differences regarding implementation.

The two organisations have been at loggerheads over Eskom’s reticence regarding a government-endorsed reform to create a separate State-owned TSO outside of Eskom, with grid assets valued at some R110-billion.

This vision was endorsed in a Phase 1 report by the Eskom Restructuring Task Team set up following President Cyril Ramaphosa’s State of the Nation Address, in which he directly contradicted an Eskom plan to create a TSO to operate the transmission system and market, but where the grid assets would remain under the ownership of an Eskom Holdings subsidiary.

Since the President’s subsequent endorsement of the Phase 1 report, BLSA reiterated its position that the creation of a separate entity, with the grid assets, was essential for levelling the playing field in an evolving competitive electricity market.

However, Eskom, mostly through its chairperson Mteto Nyati, continued to raise the risks of such a transfer for Eskom and its bondholders and persisted with the view that the TSO should be established initially without those assets.

In a joint statement the two organisations indicated that there had been “direct and constructive engagement” on the electricity reform programme and the challenges of implementing it, which had been initiated by Nyati.

“Both organisations fully support the electricity reform programme under the government's leadership, including the work of the Eskom Restructuring Task Team and the Phase 2 process now under way,” the statement reads.

“We support the outcome endorsed by the President following the Task Team's first-phase report – the establishment of an independent TSO with the transmission assets – implemented through a carefully sequenced process that safeguards Eskom's financial sustainability, respects the rights of lenders, and protects the country's energy security.

“We regard successful reform and a financially sustainable Eskom as complementary objectives, not competing ones,” it adds.

Eskom and BLSA also acknowledged that they would not always agree on every aspect of implementation, however.

“Where differences arise, we are committed to engaging directly and on the substance.

“Accelerating South Africa's economic growth rate and the jobs that depend on it require these reforms to succeed, and both organisations are committed to playing their part in making that happen.”

title: Singapore Airlines Cuts Bali Flights, Moves Key Services to 737 MAX - Aviation A2Z
description:
SINGAPORE- Singapore Airlines (SQ) will shift 3 of its 6 daily Singapore to Bali services to the Boeing 737-8 MAX for Northern Winter 2026/27.
Singapore Airlines Cuts Bali Capacity for Winter 2026/27 Singapore Airlines is making a major seasonal adjustment to its Singapore-Bali schedule from 25 October 2026.
Key Evening Services Switch to 737-8 MAX The aircraft changes affect several of the route’s most useful timings for short leisure trips.
KrisFlyer Upgrades to Business Class Singapore Airlines also lists mileage requirements for upgrading eligible Economy fares to Business Class, assuming Saver upgrade award availability.
Singapore Airlines Is Increasing Its 737 MAX Fleet The aircraft change forms part of Singapore Airlines’ broader fleet transition.
text:
SINGAPORE- Singapore Airlines (SQ) will shift 3 of its 6 daily Singapore to Bali services to the Boeing 737-8 MAX for Northern Winter 2026/27. Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) and Bali Ngurah Rai International Airport (DPS) will see half of the route’s daily rotations operated by the MAX from 25 October 2026.

The airline will also reduce the route to five daily flights for 83 of the season’s 154 days. Total winter capacity will fall 21% from the previous winter, while Business Class capacity will decline 34%. Six daily Boeing 787-10 flights are currently scheduled to return from 28 March 2027.

Singapore Airlines Cuts Bali Capacity for Winter 2026/27

Singapore Airlines is making a major seasonal adjustment to its Singapore-Bali schedule from 25 October 2026.

Three rotations will move from the 337-seat Boeing 787-10 to the 154-seat Boeing 737-8 MAX, while the other three 787-10 rotations will each have a three-week gap during the season.

The three flights moving to the Boeing 737-8 MAX are:

SQ934/935

SQ946/947

SQ948/949

The three rotations remaining on the Boeing 787-10 are:

SQ936/937

SQ938/939

SQ944/945

According to Mainly Miles, The route’s sixth daily service is also affected by the change. SQ948/949 was added as the sixth daily rotation in July 2023 and originally launched with the Boeing 737-8 MAX, so its return to the aircraft represents a restoration of its original equipment.

Singapore to Bali Flight Schedule

From 25 October 2026 to 27 March 2027, Singapore Airlines will operate the following Singapore to Bali schedule:

The return schedule from Bali is:

SQ949 operates from 26 October 2026 to 28 March 2027 because the outbound SQ948 departure from Singapore is scheduled on the previous calendar day.

Key Evening Services Switch to 737-8 MAX

The aircraft changes affect several of the route’s most useful timings for short leisure trips.

The 17:40 SQ946 and 21:30 SQ948 departures from Singapore will both use the 737-8 MAX. From 25 October 2026, the last wide-body departure available from Singapore will therefore be the 15:50 SQ944 on days when that flight operates.

The final Bali to Singapore service, SQ947 at 21:30, will also use the MAX. The two morning departures from Bali will likewise be operated by the narrow-body aircraft.

This means a typical weekend schedule involving a Friday evening departure from Singapore and a late Sunday return to Singapore will use the Boeing 737-8 MAX in both directions.

Five Daily Flights for 83 Days

The route will not maintain six daily services throughout the winter.

Singapore Airlines will operate five daily flights during 3 separate periods:

The Northern Winter 2026/27 season covers 154 days. The route will therefore operate five daily flights for 83 days, or 54% of the season.

The full 6 times daily schedule will operate for only 71 days.

Across the season, Singapore Airlines will operate 841 flights each way, compared with 924 flights during the previous winter. That is 83 fewer departures each way.

Bali Capacity Falls by 21%

The combination of fewer flights and smaller aircraft reduces total seat capacity significantly.

Business Class takes the largest proportional reduction because the Boeing 737-8 MAX has only 10 Business Class seats compared with 36 on the Boeing 787-10.

Across the season, that change reduces Business Class capacity by 9,828 seats each way, from 28,638 to 18,810.

Current Summer Capacity Is Much Higher

The winter reduction is even more pronounced when compared with the current Northern Summer 2026 schedule.

Singapore Airlines is currently operating six daily Boeing 787-10 flights, providing:

2,022 seats each way per day

216 Business Class seats each way per day

For Northern Winter 2026/27, the daily seasonal average falls to approximately:

1,316 seats each way

122 Business Class seats each way

That is approximately a 35% reduction in total daily capacity and a 43% reduction in Business Class capacity compared with the current summer schedule.

Of the 841 winter flights each way, 441 will be operated by the Boeing 737-8 MAX. The MAX will therefore account for 52% of departures, compared with 25% during the previous winter.

6 Daily Bali Flights in 2023

The 6 times daily schedule is relatively recent.

Singapore Airlines added the sixth daily Singapore-Bali rotation in July 2023. The additional service was SQ948/949, which launched on the Boeing 737-8 MAX.

The flight was scheduled with a 21:20 departure from Singapore and a 07:20 return from Bali, with timings designed partly to support long-haul connections rather than short Singapore-based weekend trips.

The sixth daily service raised Singapore Airlines and SilkAir’s combined capacity to 11,592 seats per week each way, an 18% increase from the 9,800 weekly seats they operated between them in January 2020 before COVID-19.

Singapore Airlines later increased capacity further through an all-Boeing 787-10 schedule. The current Northern Summer 2026 timetable offers a record 14,154 weekly seats each way.

The Winter 2026/27 schedule averages approximately 9,214 weekly seats each way.

That is about 20% below the level reached when the sixth daily service was introduced and around 6% below the combined Singapore Airlines and SilkAir capacity in January 2020.

Boeing 787-10 Offers More Business Class Space

The aircraft change has its greatest cabin impact in Business Class.

The Boeing 787-10 has:

36 Business Class seats

1-2-1 configuration

Direct aisle access for every passenger

Approximately 20 to 26-inch seat width

18-inch HD entertainment screens

Free Wi-Fi

Live television

The Boeing 737-8 MAX has:

10 Business Class seats

2-2, 1-1, 2-2 configuration

Approximately 19 to 22-inch seat width

16-inch HD entertainment screens

Free Wi-Fi

Live television

The 787-10 therefore provides direct aisle access from every Business Class seat. On the MAX, approximately 67% of window seats do not provide direct aisle access.

Passengers seated in 11A, 11K, 14A or 14K must pass a neighboring passenger to reach the aisle.

The MAX Has Two Solo “Throne” Seats

The two individual Business Class seats on the 737-8 MAX are 12B and 12J.

These seats provide additional space and privacy compared with the paired seats. However, there are only two on each flight.

Advance selection of the two solo seats is reserved for PPS Club members until 96 hours before departure.

Couples may prefer paired seats, while passengers traveling alone may prioritize 12B or 12J when available.

Economy Class Also Has Different Specifications

The Boeing 787-10 carries 301 Economy Class passengers, compared with 144 on the 737-8 MAX.

The 787-10 Economy Class cabin provides:

32-inch seat pitch

17.5-inch seat width

5-inch recline

11.6-inch HD entertainment screens

The 737-8 MAX provides:

30-inch seat pitch

17.7-inch seat width

5-inch recline

10-inch HD entertainment screens

Both aircraft provide free Wi-Fi and live television.

Economy Class seats on both aircraft have one USB-A socket. The aircraft also provide shared AC power arrangements.

The 737-8 MAX therefore offers slightly less legroom and smaller entertainment screens than the 787-10, although its Economy seat is marginally wider.

Business Class Still Has Fully Flat Beds

The Boeing 737-8 MAX retains fully flat Business Class beds.

The main difference is therefore not whether the seat converts into a bed, but the cabin layout, number of seats, available personal space and direct aisle access.

The 787-10 remains the stronger option for passengers who prioritize a 1-2-1 Business Class configuration.

KrisFlyer Business Class Availability

Bali has historically been one of Singapore Airlines’ more accessible KrisFlyer redemption routes, supported by six daily services and regular appearances on the airline’s monthly Spontaneous Escapes list.

The Winter 2026/27 capacity reduction changes the number of premium seats available.

Each MAX flight has only 10 Business Class seats, compared with 36 on the 787-10. Three of the six daily rotations will operate with the MAX.

The three continuing 787-10 rotations, SQ936/937, SQ938/939 and SQ944/945, therefore provide the largest Business Class cabins during the winter, although each has a three-week gap in the schedule.

Long-haul connecting passengers arriving from Europe, the United States and Australia may also compete for the limited MAX Business Class inventory.

KrisFlyer Redemption Rates for Singapore and Bali

The source lists the following one-way KrisFlyer redemption rates for Singapore-Bali:

Bali can also appear on Singapore Airlines’ monthly Spontaneous Escapes list, which offers 30% off Saver awards when the route is included.

At a 30% discount, one-way redemption rates fall to:

15,400 miles in Business Class

5,600 miles in Economy Class

Taxes, Fees and Singapore’s SAF Tax

Taxes and fees are approximately:

S$65 for Singapore to Bali

S$17 for Bali to Singapore

Bookings made from 1 October 2026 for travel on or after 1 January 2027 will also be subject to Singapore’s new Sustainable Aviation Fuel tax.

This additional charge applies to eligible bookings under the stated dates and should therefore be included when comparing the total cost of a KrisFlyer redemption.

PPS Club Members Have Additional Access

PPS Club members retain access to additional KrisFlyer award inventory.

They also retain the ability to secure the two solo Boeing 737-8 MAX Business Class seats in advance, subject to the stated 96-hour seat-selection restriction.

That provides additional access on a route where premium seating capacity will be lower during the winter season.

KrisFlyer Upgrades to Business Class

Singapore Airlines also lists mileage requirements for upgrading eligible Economy fares to Business Class, assuming Saver upgrade award availability.

The source notes that mileage upgrades are generally not an attractive proposition on this route, particularly when the Economy ticket is not being paid for by the traveler.

Singapore Airlines Is Increasing Its 737 MAX Fleet

The aircraft change forms part of Singapore Airlines’ broader fleet transition.

The airline’s Boeing 737-8 MAX fleet is expected to rise from 21 to 26 aircraft following five deliveries during the financial year. That represents a 24% increase and takes the airline closer to its 29 aircraft order after years of Boeing production delays.

At the same time, Singapore Airlines’ long-haul fleet is shrinking for the first time in six years.

The additional MAX aircraft therefore need to be deployed across regional markets. The aircraft is suited to sectors of roughly 1 to 6 hours, while the Singapore-Bali flight takes about two hours and 45 minutes.

The same fleet strategy is appearing elsewhere. The Boeing 737-8 MAX is scheduled to serve Manila from August 2026, while Cairns is due to receive daily MAX service from December 2026, replacing larger aircraft on that route.

Six Boeing 787-10 Flights Return in March 2027

The published schedule currently shows a return to full wide-body operation from 28 March 2027.

From that date, Singapore Airlines is scheduled to operate six daily Boeing 787-10 flights between Singapore and Bali, restoring the route to the same full wide-body operation currently used during Northern Summer 2026.

The pattern is consistent with Singapore Airlines deploying larger regional aircraft during Bali’s stronger Northern Summer demand and reducing capacity during the quieter Northern Winter period.

The Summer 2027 aircraft allocation remains provisional. Singapore Airlines typically finalizes future aircraft assignments closer to the operating season, often around December or January, so the published schedule can still change.

Winter Changes Mean for Travelers

The Winter 2026/27 schedule will provide substantially less capacity than the current summer operation.

Three of six daily flights will use the Boeing 737-8 MAX, the route will operate five daily flights for 83 days, and total winter capacity will fall 21% from the previous winter.

Business Class passengers face the largest reduction, with capacity down 34% for the season. The 787-10’s 36-seat 1-2-1 cabin provides a materially different experience from the MAX’s 10-seat 2-2, 1-1, 2-2 configuration.

Travelers seeking Business Class should therefore prioritize SQ936/937, SQ938/939 and SQ944/945 when those services are operating the 787-10.

Those flights remain subject to three-week gaps during the winter, so travelers need to check the aircraft and operating date before booking.

Conclusion

Singapore Airlines will move three of its six daily Singapore-Bali rotations to the Boeing 737-8 MAX from 25 October 2026 and reduce the route to five daily services for 83 of 154 winter days.

The resulting Winter 2026/27 schedule will provide 841 flights and 202,714 seats each way, compared with 924 flights and 258,193 seats in the previous winter. Business Class capacity will fall from 28,638 to 18,810 seats, a 34% reduction.

More than half of all winter flights, 441 of 841, will use the Boeing 737-8 MAX. The three 787-10 rotations will retain the larger Business Class cabin and direct aisle access, but each will have a three-week operating gap.

Singapore Airlines currently plans to restore six daily Boeing 787-10 flights from 28 March 2027, returning the Singapore-Bali route to full wide-body operation.

text:
For Canadian agricultural equipment dealers and repair shops, keeping customers operating has never been more challenging.

Today’s farms rely on increasingly diverse equipment fleets, often combining machines from multiple manufacturers and generations. Supporting those fleets requires access to a wide range of replacement parts without adding complexity to an already demanding service environment.

GRANIT PARTS Canada launched back in February 2026 to help address those challenges by giving dealers and repair shops access to a broad assortment of agricultural replacement parts through a single supplier relationship.

GRANIT PARTS simplifies the parts-sourcing process. The company positions itself as a single source for agricultural parts, aiming to provide every item a farmer might need to remain profitable.

Kabir says working with a supplier that offers access to parts across major equipment brands can help dealers and repair shops streamline purchasing processes, reduce the number of supplier relationships they need to manage and spend more time focused on serving customers.

The opportunity extends beyond operational efficiency. “Parts sourcing is more than supply and operational necessity. Every single day it’s about creating an advantage by strengthening customer relationships,” says Kabir.

Founded in 1996 as a subsidiary of the Fricke Group, GRANIT PARTS Canada gives Canadian dealers and repair shops access to a catalogue of more than 14 million items, with approximately 250,000 part numbers available for immediate shipment at any given time.

Built for uptime

Current economic conditions have prompted many farmers to keep equipment in service longer, increasing demand for repair and replacement parts. As more producers choose to maintain and rebuild existing machinery rather than purchase new equipment, dealers and repair shops need confidence that the parts they require will be available when needed.

Kabir says uptime remains the priority.

“Agriculture doesn’t wait. When equipment is down, every hour matters. Dealers need partners who understand that urgency and are built to respond.”

That means more than simply offering a large catalogue. Consistent inventory, dependable delivery and reliable ordering processes are essential because dealers need assurance they can access parts quickly and keep customers operating during critical farming windows.

For repair shops and dealerships, minimizing downtime helps protect customer productivity while reinforcing trust and long-term business relationships.

Private brands fill market gaps

For GRANIT PARTS, the aftermarket opportunity is about more than supplying replacement parts. The company has developed proprietary product lines aimed at solving performance challenges identified in the field.

One example is the company’s Endurance Till line. Its ripper points use premium white iron material and optimized wing placement to improve hard pan fracture performance.

“When we moved our wing forward on the point, it ended up pulling a bit harder and did a much better job fracturing that hard pan under the ground so it could perform like it was supposed to,” says Fleck.

GRANIT PARTS’ Exact Align system addresses precision issues in planter row units by replacing traditional bushings with ball bearings for smoother, more consistent performance.

“We’ve been doing this for about seven years now and they are still in the field,” says Fleck.

Digital tools make ordering easy

GRANIT PARTS also invests heavily in digital tools designed to make finding and ordering parts faster and more accurate for dealers and repair shops.

“In the parts business, digitalization directly impacts availability and service,” says Farhan Kabir.

The company’s online platform allows users to search by serial number, access interactive parts diagrams and add components directly to their cart. The Granit mobile app offers similar capabilities and can even identify equivalent Granit replacement parts by scanning competitor part numbers.

According to Kabir, digital ordering helps reduce manual steps, minimize errors and give dealers more control over the purchasing process.

“At GRANIT PARTS, around 97% of all orders are already processed digitally,” he says. Kabir emphasizes that technology is only part of the customer experience.

“Of course, digitalization doesn’t replace service. But it makes good service at scale possible.”

Global strength, personal support

That combination of technology and service reflects the broader philosophy of the Fricke Group, which remains family-owned after more than a century in business.

The company is led by Hans-Peter Fricke, the third generation of family ownership. While the organization has grown into a global agricultural parts supplier with thousands of employees, it continues to emphasize direct customer relationships.

For Canadian dealers and repair shops, that means access to the resources, inventory and expertise of a global organization, combined with dedicated support focused on the needs of the Canadian market.

Canadian dealers and repair shops attending Canada’s Outdoor Farm Show, Sept. 15 to 17, 2026, can also meet the GRANIT PARTS Canada team at Booth #731 to learn more about the company’s replacement parts solutions and support for the Canadian market.

text:
What's the deal? Atierra, an OIST-born startup developing microalgae-derived low-carbon feedstocks for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), has closed a 60,000,000 JPY (about $374,722) pre-seed round. The OIST-Lifetime Ventures Fund and Lifetime Ventures led, with Yuri Group, Shinryo Fund, and angel investors participating.

Atierra, founded by chief executive officer Shivani Sathish and co-founder Daniel Yee, is building a microalgae bioproduction platform to produce low-carbon oils for SAF at lower cost and larger scale. The company aims to commercialise sustainable, price-competitive feedstocks — a supply gap it calls a key bottleneck to wider SAF adoption.

Where the money goes: Atierra will focus on validating its bioproduction technology, building partnerships across the SAF value chain, strengthening its intellectual property strategy, and preparing for pilot deployment and its next equity round.

Why now? Aviation is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonise, and demand for SAF is rising. "As SAF demand grows, the challenge is translating that potential into stable, cost-competitive, large-scale production," Sathish said.

Why microalgae? "Microalgae is one of the few feedstocks that can deliver SAF at the scale aviation needs," said Kureaki Kunii, representative partner at Lifetime Ventures, pointing to Atierra's "interdisciplinary" and "AI-native" approach.

The signal: At roughly $375,000, the round sits near the smaller end for the sector — around the 21st percentile by size. The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) has announced up to $105.6 million in funding for 20 research and development projects aimed at reducing the cost of designing, building, operating and maintaining large-scale solar farms.

According to ARENA, the investment is its largest single commitment to solar photovoltaic research and development and supports projects focused on improving the efficiency, cost and stability of advanced solar cells and modules, as well as reducing the levelised cost of electricity from solar farms.

The funding builds on ARENA’s ultra low-cost solar ambition, which aims to reduce installed solar costs to 30 cents per watt by 2030.

ARENA acting CEO Chris Faris said the projects were intended to address challenges across the solar technology value chain.

“Australia has played a leading role in the development of solar technology, and these projects will help ensure we continue to strengthen that position,” Faris said.

“The portfolio brings together a mix of near-term improvements and breakthrough technologies that have the potential to lower costs, improve performance and accelerate the deployment of solar energy both in Australia and around the world.”

The projects are divided into two streams. The first focuses on solar cells and modules, including efforts to increase efficiency, reduce costs and improve stability. The second covers balance-of-system technologies and operations and maintenance, with projects targeting lower deployment and maintenance costs and improved solar energy yields.

Recipients include the Australian National University, UNSW, the University of Melbourne, the University of Sydney and several companies, including Sunspence Pty Ltd and Proa Energy Australia Pty Ltd.

Faris said ARENA increased the funding pool from its initial allocation of $60 million following the response to the funding round.

“ARENA initially allocated $60 million to the Ultra Low-Cost Solar PV Research and Development Funding Round,” he said. “When we saw the quality of applications, we decided to increase funding to support a broader portfolio of high-quality projects that can help accelerate progress towards ultra low-cost solar.”

The funded projects include research into perovskite and silicon tandem cells, solar module durability, artificial intelligence-assisted materials discovery, utility-scale PV reliability and solar farm operations and maintenance.

According to ARENA, the portfolio is intended to support innovation across the solar value chain as Australia seeks to reduce the cost of solar-generated electricity.

title: Beneath the Surface: Australian clean fuels consultation - CMEWA
description:

text:
The Australian Government has published a consultation on measures to stimulate investment in cleaner fuels, including biofuels such as renewable diesel and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). This was part of a wider announcement on fuel resilience, which also included proposals to bolster Australia’s security of traditional fuels like diesel.

This year’s events in the Strait of Hormuz have sharpened the focus on our fuel security, but cleaner fuels are also an easy way to reduce emissions. Because they are chemically the same as the fossil fuels they aim to replace, they can be used as a ‘drop in’ fuel without having to adopt any new technologies or invest in new infrastructure. There is a potential for products like renewable diesel to support decarbonisation across the economy, including agriculture, haulage and defence. SAF is generally seen as the only viable means for the airline industry to meet net zero by 2050.

For the resources sector, renewable fuels could play a part in near-term decarbonisation of mines and bulk haulage, ahead of large-scale electrification which itself will depend on new technologies being deployed and the build out of renewable power grids. They may also play a part in remote facilities or ones which have a short asset life, where electrification is not viable.

However, these fuels currently come at a significant premium: in part because of their novelty, but largely due to the limitations on their domestic supply. Domestic production of renewable diesel is currently limited to a few small-scale demonstration projects, and what we do use is imported.

The WA Government is expected to finalise an Advanced Biofuels Strategy later this year which should aim to support domestic biofuel production, taking advantage of agricultural waste from the Wheatbelt. This would complement the Federal Government’s $1.1 billion Cleaner Fuels Program, announced in September 2025, which similarly aims to attract investment in domestic production.

CME supports these government-led, domestic supply-side measures. With increased scale, the price premium in comparison to fossil fuels should reduce.

However, the consultation makes clear that the Federal Government also wants to impose renewable fuel mandates to drive demand, in parallel with support for supply. The nature of these mandates is up for discussion, but it would effectively require a percentage of fuel to come from renewable sources – possibly as soon as in three years’ time. This approach is taken in other countries jurisdictions such as the EU, UK and Canada. The UK requires 14 per cent of fuel sold at the bowser and 10 per cent of aviation fuel to be renewable.

CME is concerned about the near-term cost of potential mandates. WA’s resources sector is heavily reliant on diesel, accounting for 43 per cent of Australia’s resource sector diesel consumption. Even a small mandate may drive cost increases, particularly in early years when supply is limited and new production projects are recouping investment costs. Notably, the Australian Government has not yet carried out an assessment of this impact on the resources sector (or indeed the economy more generally).

CME’s view is that decarbonisation policies should not direct individual industrial facilities on how they should decarbonise. For the majority of the sector, mandating the use of renewable fuels will drive up costs just as investments in electrification – the real prize – are being made, and could even put those investments at risk.

CME will be arguing in its submission that efforts to develop a domestic supply of renewable fuels should not be coupled with mandates, until the cost of renewable fuels is brought down to a par of fossil fuels.

text:
As one of the key partners supporting KMITL EXPO 2026, Bangchak Group has delivered 1,000 liters of green diesel, or Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO), produced in Thailand for the first time to King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang (KMITL). The fuel will be used in shuttle vehicles for visitors attending the event at KMITL from 1-6 September 2026. Bangchak Group will also purchase used cooking oil generated during the event for conversion into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

KMITL EXPO 2026 will mark the first use of HVO produced in Thailand. A drop-in biofuel, HVO can be used in compatible diesel engines and existing fuel infrastructure without major modifications. It helps reduce dependence on fossil fuels and imported oil while supporting greater use of renewable feedstocks available in Thailand. The HVO supplied to KMITL is produced at the same production unit as SAF within the Bangchak Phra Khanong Refinery. The unit can adjust its production process and product slate to produce fuels suited to both road and air transport, using used cooking oil as feedstock. Replacing fossil fuel with HVO can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 2.58 kgCO2e, or kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent, per liter. The 1,000 liters of HVO used in the event’s shuttle vehicles are therefore expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 2.58 tCO2e, or metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent. Bangchak Group will also purchase used cooking oil from within the event through its “Fry to Fly” initiative and use it as feedstock for SAF production.

Using locally produced HVO in event shuttles while collecting used cooking oil for SAF production connects road and air transport through a circular use of resources. It brings the “From Lab to Life” concept to life by putting Thailand’s renewable feedstocks, technology, and production capabilities into practical, everyday use.

KMITL EXPO 2026 is organized by KMITL to welcome school and university students, families, and everyone interested in technology and creativity. Visitors can experience, test, and interact with research-based innovations designed for practical application across 10 innovation pavilions under the theme “From Lab to Life.” The event will take place at KMITL from 1-6 September 2026.

text:
The 2026 Aviation Industry Career Expo, bringing together future job opportunities across the aviation sector, will be held at BEXCO in Busan over two days beginning Wednesday.

Hosted by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, the expo is the first to be held in the southeastern region and combines the aviation industry job fair and the aviation leisure industry job fair into a single event.

More than 100 companies and organizations spanning the full range of the aviation industry will take part, covering air transport, airport operations, maintenance, repair and overhaul, and ground handling, as well as drones, urban air mobility, sustainable aviation fuel and aviation leisure.

To give job seekers practical assistance, the expo will link a career exploration zone, an AI matching zone and an on-site hiring zone into a one-stop process, allowing visitors to gather information, explore options and sit for interviews all in one place.

A range of side events designed for young job seekers to participate in and enjoy will also be on offer. Hands-on activities include guessing baggage weight, learning ground crew hand signals, identifying aviation radio communication terms, an aviation golden bell quiz and an OX quiz. Competitive programs will include an aviation safety speech contest and an aviation industry idea competition.

Jeong Chae-gyo, director general for aviation policy at the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, said he hoped the expo would "provide a wide range of employment opportunities in the aviation field for young people and other job seekers, and serve as an opportunity to strengthen the competitiveness of our aviation industry."

Niutech SAF Agreement: A Bold Waste-to-Fuel Move

Updated: August 29, 2026

Niutech Technology Group says it has signed an agreement to supply an industrial waste-plastic pyrolysis line to a major international energy company.

According to the Chinese equipment manufacturer, the system will be installed as part of an upgrade at one of the customer’s large refineries. The proposed production chain would convert waste plastic into pyrolysis oil before upgrading that oil through hydrotreatment into aviation fuel.

The announcement could open another route for producing lower-carbon aviation fuel from difficult waste streams. However, several important details remain undisclosed, including the customer’s identity, the contract value, the construction schedule and the certification pathway for the finished fuel. Niutech SAF agreement

What has Niutech announced?

Niutech says its new customer has ordered an industrial continuous waste-plastic pyrolysis production line with a processing capacity of between 10,000 and 50,000 tonnes per year.

The agreement represents Niutech’s first entry into the unidentified company’s equipment supply chain, according to the company-issued announcement distributed by PR Newswire.

Niutech has not named the energy company. It also has not published the refinery’s location, the exact capacity selected by the customer or a date for commissioning the equipment.

These omissions mean that the announcement should presently be understood as a supplier’s account of a commercial agreement—not as confirmation that SAF production has begun.

How would the process work?

Pyrolysis heats plastic in a low-oxygen environment, breaking its molecules into products that include liquid oil, gas and solid residue.

Niutech says its continuous system can process polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, ABS, nylon and certain mixed-plastic streams. The company also claims the line can accept some low-value plastics without the extensive washing, drying and sorting required by other processes.

The resulting pyrolysis oil is not finished aviation fuel. It must undergo additional refining and hydrotreatment, and the final product must meet the technical, sustainability and safety requirements applicable in its target market.

That distinction matters: a facility capable of producing pyrolysis oil is one part of a longer production and certification chain. Niutech SAF agreement

Why is the project connected to SAF demand?

Aviation remains difficult to decarbonize because long-distance aircraft require fuels with high energy density. Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is therefore expected to play a significant role alongside more efficient aircraft, operational improvements and emerging propulsion technologies.

The European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation rules require aviation-fuel suppliers at covered EU airports to deliver a minimum SAF share of 2% from 2025. The requirement rises to 6% in 2030 and 70% in 2050, according to the official EU regulation.

The regulation can recognize certain fuels made from non-renewable waste streams as recycled carbon aviation fuels, subject to its definitions and sustainability requirements. A plastic-derived fuel does not qualify merely because waste plastic was used as an input.

Its eligibility depends on factors such as the nature of the waste, the production pathway, lifecycle greenhouse-gas performance, traceability and regulatory certification.

Could plastic-derived fuel complement used cooking oil?

Used cooking oil and waste fats are established SAF feedstocks, but their sustainable supply is limited. This has encouraged producers to investigate additional waste-derived and synthetic pathways.

Waste-plastic pyrolysis could broaden the feedstock base, particularly for material that cannot reasonably be reused or mechanically recycled. It may also help divert some residual plastic from landfill or uncontrolled disposal.

Nevertheless, environmental performance cannot be assumed. The energy consumed during pyrolysis and upgrading, the source of that energy, transportation requirements, process yields and treatment of by-products all affect lifecycle emissions.

Priority should also remain with waste prevention, reuse and mechanical recycling where those options are technically and environmentally preferable.

What remains unknown about the Niutech SAF agreement?

The announcement leaves several questions unanswered:

Who is the energy customer?

Where will the equipment be installed?

What is the contract’s financial value?

When will construction and commissioning take place?

Which waste streams will supply the facility?

What percentage of the pyrolysis oil could become aviation fuel?

Which fuel standard and sustainability scheme will apply?

What independently reviewed emissions savings are expected?

Has an aviation-fuel producer or certification body approved the proposed pathway?

Until these details are released, claims about production volumes or climate benefits would be premature. Niutech SAF agreement

What experience does Niutech bring?

Niutech, listed in Shanghai under stock code 688309, develops continuous pyrolysis equipment for waste plastics, scrap tyres, oily sludge and other waste streams.

The company says its technology has been deployed in markets including China, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand and Vietnam. Those deployment claims come from Niutech and were not accompanied in the latest announcement by project-level production data or independent operating assessments.

Its experience with continuous processing may be commercially relevant because large plants must maintain stable temperatures, control emissions and handle changes in feedstock composition over extended operating periods.

What happens next?

The agreement is an early commercial signal rather than proof of operating SAF production.

The most meaningful milestones will be disclosure of the customer and project location, delivery of the equipment, refinery commissioning, verified lifecycle-emissions results and certification of the finished fuel.

If those steps are completed successfully, the project could demonstrate how non-recyclable plastic waste may serve as an upstream source for recycled carbon aviation fuel. Until then, Niutech’s announcement is best viewed as a potentially important—but still developing—industrial project. Niutech SAF agreement

Key facts

Announcement date: August 29, 2026

Supplier: Niutech Technology Group

Customer: Undisclosed global energy company

Equipment: Continuous waste-plastic pyrolysis line

Stated annual capacity: 10,000–50,000 tonnes per unit

Intermediate product: Waste-plastic pyrolysis oil

Intended downstream product: Hydrotreated aviation fuel

Contract value: Not disclosed

Project location: Not disclosed

Production start: Not disclosed

SAF certification: Not disclosed

title: Why Boeing Dispatched a Senior Executive to a Rolls-Royce Factory - ePlaneAI
description:
The Trent 1000 Crisis and Boeing’s Unprecedented Response Rolls-Royce has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past decade.
This turnaround contrasts sharply with the crisis that engulfed the company ten years ago, when persistent problems with its Trent 1000 engine led to widespread groundings of Boeing 787 Dreamliners.
The severity of the Trent 1000 issues compelled Boeing to take an extraordinary measure: sending a senior executive, a vice president, directly to a Rolls-Royce factory.
This rare intervention aimed to address the durability problems afflicting the Trent 1000 engines, which powered many 787 Dreamliners.

text:
The Trent 1000 Crisis and Boeing’s Unprecedented Response

Rolls-Royce has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past decade. In July, the aircraft engine manufacturer reported a significant increase in interim operating profit, raised its full-year earnings forecast, and assured airline customers that engine or parts shortages causing aircraft groundings were now a thing of the past. This turnaround contrasts sharply with the crisis that engulfed the company ten years ago, when persistent problems with its Trent 1000 engine led to widespread groundings of Boeing 787 Dreamliners. The resulting saga inflicted billions in losses on Rolls-Royce and severely tarnished its reputation.

The severity of the Trent 1000 issues compelled Boeing to take an extraordinary measure: sending a senior executive, a vice president, directly to a Rolls-Royce factory. This rare intervention aimed to address the durability problems afflicting the Trent 1000 engines, which powered many 787 Dreamliners. By stationing a top Boeing executive on-site, the company sought to expedite solutions, stabilize production schedules, and reassure both airline operators and investors that the crisis was being managed effectively. Market reactions to Boeing’s involvement were mixed. Some analysts commended the proactive stance as a demonstration of Boeing’s commitment to its customers and partners, while others interpreted it as evidence of the complex interdependence—and underlying competitive tension—between the two aerospace giants.

Origins of the Crisis: Design Choices and Weight Challenges

To fully grasp the origins of the crisis, it is necessary to revisit the early 2000s, when Boeing embarked on designing the next-generation 787 Dreamliner. The company commissioned engines from both GE Aerospace and Rolls-Royce, imposing stringent requirements for fuel efficiency and weight. Notably, Boeing instructed both manufacturers not to “oversize” their engines, diverging from the conventional practice of building in extra capacity to accommodate potential changes during aircraft development.

When Japan’s All Nippon Airways (ANA) placed the first order in 2004, Rolls-Royce’s Trent 1000 was selected, and the 787 program officially commenced. However, by the time the 787-8 and 787-9 variants were certified and entered service, the aircraft were significantly heavier than initially projected—503,000 lbs (228,000 kg) and 558,000 lbs (253,000 kg), respectively, compared to original estimates of 452,000 lbs (205,000 kg) and 485,000 lbs (220,000 kg). This discrepancy placed unforeseen stress on the engines, particularly the Trent 1000, resulting in premature wear and ultimately forcing the grounding of dozens of aircraft.

Industry Implications and Lessons Learned

Boeing’s decision to embed a senior executive at the Rolls-Royce factory underscored the urgency of resolving these technical challenges. The move was critical not only to restore confidence among airline customers but also to prevent further disruptions to the 787 program. While competitors observed the situation closely, the episode highlighted the intense competition and mutual reliance that characterize the modern aerospace industry.

Today, with the Trent 1000 issues largely resolved and Rolls-Royce’s financial position strengthened, both companies appear to have drawn important lessons from the crisis. The episode remains a stark reminder of the complexities and risks inherent in developing cutting-edge aviation technology, as well as the extraordinary measures industry leaders will undertake to safeguard their interests and reputations.

text:
The global airline industry is expected to remain profitable in 2026, but rising fuel costs, geopolitical disruptions and aircraft shortages are threatening to weaken its post-pandemic recovery. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) forecasts that airlines worldwide will record combined net profits of USD23 billion this year, down from an estimated $45 billion in 2025.

As a result, the industry’s net profit margin is projected to fall from 4.2% last year to just 2%, despite expected revenues of approximately $1.165 trillion.

Erik Chan, IATA’s area manager for Hong Kong and Macau, presented the figures during a France Macau Chamber of Commerce (FMCC)Breakfast Talk Rendez-Vous last week and offered his perspective.

Chan has more than 15 years of experience working with international carriers, including Cathay Pacific and Qatar Airways.

IATA represents more than 370 airlines, accounting for approximately 85% of global air traffic.

Growth slows as costs rise

Despite the increasingly challenging financial outlook this year, Chan said passenger demand remained resilient. “Luckily in our region in Asia Pacific, we can see that […] in this region that the prices goes up and still demand is strong,” he said.

Regional growth, however, is expected to remain uneven, he added.

Asia-Pacific is forecast to lead, with passenger traffic increasing by about 5%, while North America grows by less than 1%.

Meanwhile, the Middle East has suffered the most severe contraction. That regional outlook has since been affected by higher fuel prices and disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.

There, passenger load factors fell from 80.8% to 77.2% by April as airspace restrictions and rerouted flights disrupted established networks.

Even so, Chan said the disruption had shifted traffic rather than eliminated it.

Chan detailed that Middle Eastern carriers’ share of certain Asia-Europe transfer markets had fallen from 26% to 13%, while Asian and European airlines captured much of the displaced demand.

“Traffic still grows,” Chan said. “What changed is the cost of flying people […] This is what a network does: block one path, and the flow finds another,” he said.

That rerouting, however, comes at a steep price.

Chan said rising costs were being driven largely by fuel, citing jet fuel prices of about $152 a barrel and noting that every additional hour in the air adds significantly to airline expenses. Moreover, fuel is expected to account for roughly 31% of airline operating costs in 2026, up from 25% the previous year.

On passenger fares, prices are expected to climb by nearly 8%, according to the IATA figures.

Aircraft shortages limit expansion

Also hindering airline growth is the shortage of new aircraft. Carriers are struggling to expand because manufacturers cannot deliver planes quickly enough.

Chan said the gap between expected deliveries and the pre-pandemic trend has reached about 5,600 aircraft, while the global order backlog represents roughly 12 years of production at the current pace.

This shortage is limiting airlines’ ability to add routes, replace older aircraft and reduce fuel consumption. The impact is particularly significant in Asia-Pacific, where domestic travel has become a major driver of global growth, Chan highlighted.

To illustrate the shift, Chan presented figures showing that the United States accounted for roughly two-thirds of the world’s domestic air travel in 2000, while China represented about 6%. Today, the U.S. share is slightly above one-third, China’s is close to 29% and India’s has risen from about 1% to 5%.

“With just only 25 years that’s passed […] you can see the gigantic power of China is happening; within the China domestic line is growing a lot, and the emerging sectors from India is also happening around the globe. That is one of the largest structural shifts in the industry’s history, and it took only 25 years,” Chan remarked.

And that transformation is likely to continue.

IATA projects that global passenger demand will more than double by 2050 – rising from about 9 trillion revenue passenger kilometers (RPK) in 2024 to between 19.5 trillion and 21.9 trillion, depending on the growth scenario.

Meanwhile, air cargo growth has slowed to about 0.7% in 2026, from an earlier forecast of 2.1%.

Yet, cargo yields are rising because the loss of passenger flights has removed valuable belly-hold capacity.

Cargo demand remains selective

“Most air power does not fly on freighters. It travels in the belly of passenger aircraft […] the Gulf carriers fly very large, wide-body fleets on exactly the routes where the belly space matters most,” Chan said, adding, “When the passenger shadow stopped, about 30% of the world’s cargo capacity stopped with them.”

“So, this is a supply cut, not a demand cut.”

Chan then shifted to trade in artificial intelligence-related goods – including servers, chips and other components. He said that these products are generating significant demand in his industry.

Chan also said the value of that trade had increased from about $2 trillion in 2015 to nearly $4 trillion today.

AI-related goods account for only about 7% of air cargo by weight, but they represent more than half of its value, Chan said.

“More than two thirds of it moves by air. So now, reverse that view by weight. […] a small number of light, expensive boxes now account for most of the value that holds,” adding that, “These economics are simple.”

Net zero depends on fuel

The end of the session examined the aviation industry’s path toward net-zero emissions by 2050. Chan said IATA is promoting sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, produced from sources including used cooking oil and other alternative feedstocks.

SAF currently represents less than 1% of global aviation fuel use. IATA expects production to reach about 2.4 million tons in 2026, equivalent to only 0.8% of total aviation fuel consumption.

Chan said that Hong Kong has a target of 1% to 2% SAF use over the next three years, while Singapore is pursuing a target of about 10% within five years.

Chan also said the Hong Kong government is working with mainland authorities on a proposed SAF production facility in the Greater Bay Area.

However, SAF remains substantially more expensive than conventional jet fuel and currently can be blended at levels of up to 50% in commercial aircraft.

Moreover, current market tracking shows that SAF generally costs between 2 and 5 times more than fossil jet fuel. In some mandated European and Asian markets, the premium pushes SAF prices as high as $2,830–$2,872 per metric ton, whereas conventional jet fuel averages closer to $1,400 per ton.

Whether SAF is a viable way forward depends on how the aviation sector scales up production, manages costs, and navigates policy requirements. The transition remains at an early stage.

title: Turning Emissions Data into a Competitive Advantage - Air Cargo Week
description:
Turning Emissions Data into a Competitive Advantage For many logistics businesses, decarbonisation begins with operational change.
Marken’s approach aims to show that meaningful emissions reduction can begin elsewhere: with trusted data, consistent methodology and a clear understanding of where emissions originate.
“We aim to ensure all Marken customers benefit from a baseline reduction in transport emissions across our network.
Organisations able to provide transparent, independently supported emissions data can gain an advantage in commercial discussions, particularly with customers pursuing their own Science Based Targets.
“With what we have built, including supplier relationships, verified data and external assurance, we can respond to client needs and compete confidently with industry peers.
text:
Marken established shipment-level emissions transparency using recognised standards, giving it an auditable view of emissions across a complex network of transport partners and identifying credible reduction opportunities.

Marken works with airlines and road carriers to introduce Sustainable Aviation Fuel and Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil, with reductions tied to physical fuel investments and verified claims.

Verified data, external assurance and measurable Scope 3 reductions help Marken support customers’ sustainability targets, strengthen procurement discussions and differentiate the business competitively.

Turning Emissions Data into a Competitive Advantage

For many logistics businesses, decarbonisation begins with operational change. For healthcare logistics providers, the equation is more complex. Time-critical biological samples, patient-specific therapies and temperature-sensitive products leave little room to replace airfreight with slower, lower-carbon transport. Marken’s approach aims to show that meaningful emissions reduction can begin elsewhere: with trusted data, consistent methodology and a clear understanding of where emissions originate.

Before introducing a customer-facing Low Emission Transport offering, Marken invested in shipment-level emissions transparency aligned with recognised standards, creating an auditable baseline capable of supporting corporate targets and customer reporting.

“When we stepped back from the detail, we could see how far we had come,” said Sandra Voss, Director Global Sustainability at Marken. “The data foundation, supplier relationships and verified reductions were achievements we could genuinely be proud of. The partnership with shipzero was essential in making that possible.”

The experience highlights how operational visibility becomes a prerequisite for strategic action when emissions are distributed across complex supply chains.

“Operating through hundreds of transport partners meant building that emissions picture was a substantial challenge,” Voss explained. “Only then could we identify credible reduction opportunities.”

Turning supplier relationships into measurable reductions

Once a credible baseline existed, Marken shifted its focus towards influencing the supply chain rather than redesigning it. Working directly with contracted airlines and road carriers, the company supported the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel and Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil within its transport network.

This distinction matters. Reductions remain connected to the physical supply chain rather than relying on external carbon credits, strengthening credibility and traceability.

Marken allocates baseline reductions across eligible shipments while offering dedicated verified claim certificates to customers that co-invest in emission reduction initiatives. This approach extends the benefits of network-wide improvements while maintaining accounting integrity and avoiding double counting.

“We aim to ensure all Marken customers benefit from a baseline reduction in transport emissions across our network. Customers can also work towards their own Scope 3 targets by participating in our co-investment programme and receiving verified claim certificates for the reductions they support,” Voss said. “We engage exclusively with the airlines and carriers that actually transport our shipments on implementing SAF and HVO within their own networks. Every reduction is linked to a real fuel investment within our supply chain.”

From compliance requirement to commercial differentiator

As customer expectations around Scope 3 reporting intensify, verified emissions reductions are becoming more than a compliance exercise. They increasingly influence procurement decisions, competitive positioning and customer relationships. Organisations able to provide transparent, independently supported emissions data can gain an advantage in commercial discussions, particularly with customers pursuing their own Science Based Targets.

Asset-light businesses across global supply chains often have limited direct operational control, making supplier engagement critical. Book & Claim provides a mechanism for rewarding investment in lower-emission fuels while giving customers measurable outcomes that fit recognised reporting frameworks.

“With what we have built, including supplier relationships, verified data and external assurance, we can respond to client needs and compete confidently with industry peers. Most importantly, we can report credible progress against our corporate commitments,” Voss concluded. “Don’t wait for the perfect solution,” she concluded. “Start with the first step and be transparent about where you are.”

N.D.

Prin intermediul unui comunicat de presă, OMV Petrom a anunțat că extinde capacitatea de producție de hidrogen verde la rafinăria Petrobrazi din județul Prahova. ”OMV Petrom, cel mai mare producător integrat de energie din Europa de Sud-Est, anunță livrarea tuturor celor șapte module pentru cel de-al doilea său electrolizor de hidrogen verde, cu o capacitate de 35 MW, la rafinăria Petrobrazi. Alături de instalația de 20 MW anunțată anterior, capacitatea totală instalată de producție a hidrogenului verde la Petrobrazi se ridică acum la 55 MW”, se precizează în comunicatul de presă. Potrivit reprezentanților companiei, atingerea unei capacități de producție de 55 MW de hidrogen verde pentru rafinăria Petrobrazi este un pas important, având în vedere faptul că hidrogenul verde va fi utilizat în procesele de rafinare, inclusiv pentru producția de combustibil sustenabil pentru aviație (SAF –sustainable aviation fuel) și motorină din surse regenerabile (HVO – hydrotreated vegetable oil), contribuind la reducerea emisiilor acestor combustibili față de alternativele convenționale. Cel de-al doilea proiect de hidrogen verde este format din șapte module de electroliză de câte 5 MW fiecare, furnizate de o firmă din Germania, acestea fiind livrate în Prahova, la Petrobrazi, în ultimele două luni și sunt deja integrate în infrastructura rafinăriei. Proiectul de 35 MW beneficiază de aproximativ 29 de milioane de euro finanțare nerambursabilă prin Planul Național de Redresare și Reziliență al României (PNRR), iar odată operațional, se estimează că se vor produce anual aproximativ 4.700 de tone de hidrogen verde din energie electrică din surse regenerabile, pentru noua unitate ce va produce combustibil sustenabil pentru aviație și motorină din surse regenerabile, aflată în construcție tot la Petrobrazi. ”Cele două proiecte de hidrogen verde, cu o capacitate totală instalată de 55 MW și o producție anuală estimată de aproximativ 8.000 de tone, vor fi folosite în procesele de rafinare, inclusiv în producția de combustibili sustenabili SAF și HVO, obținuți din uleiuri vegetale și uleiuri uzate. Acești combustibili pot reduce emisiile de CO₂ cu cel puțin 65% pe întregul ciclu de viață și sunt compatibili cu infrastructura existentă. În paralel, avansăm construcția unității SAF/HVO cu o capacitate de 250.000 de tone pe an, care va poziționa OMV Petrom drept primul producător major de combustibili sustenabili din Europa de Sud-Est. OMV Petrom este cel mai mare producător integrat de energie din Europa de Sud-Est, cu o producție anuală de țiței și gaze la nivel de grup de aproximativ 38 milioane bep în 2025. Grupul are o capacitate de rafinare de 4,5 milioane tone anual și operează o centrală electrică pe gaze naturale de înaltă eficiență de 860 MW”, s-a mai menționat în comunicat.
