text:
JINAN, China, Aug. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd. (abbreviated as "Niutech"), a global supplier of industrial continuous pyrolysis solutions, has signed a sales contract with a global energy major for an Industrial Continuous Waste Plastic Pyrolysis Production Line. Featuring Niutech's proprietary technology and single-unit capacity of 10,000 to 50,000 tons per year (tpy), the line will upgrade one of the customer's large-scale refineries, enabling end-to-end production from waste plastic pyrolysis oil to hydrotreated Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). This marks Niutech's first entry into the customer's equipment supply chain.

SAF is a critical pathway for aviation decarbonization. The EU's ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation mandates a 2% SAF blend from 2025, rising to 6% by 2030 and 70% by 2050. With Used Cooking Oil (UCO) supply limited, waste plastic-to-SAF is emerging as a promising second route. Niutech's technology converts low-value waste plastics — including PP, PE, PS, ABS and nylon, single-type or mixed — directly into pyrolysis oil suitable for SAF, without complex pre-treatment such as washing, sorting or drying.

The company's waste plastic pyrolysis solutions have been commercially deployed across the UK, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand, Vietnam and China, delivering multiple 10,000-tpy-class continuous pyrolysis projects.

"Large-scale pyrolysis projects impose stringent requirements on continuous operational capability," said a Niutech marketing executive. "Niutech has focused on pyrolysis technology for nearly 40 years and brings mature equipment and extensive project experience. This partnership is another validation of the strength of our industrial continuous technology."

About Niutech

Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd. (Stock Code: 688309) is an integrated pyrolysis solution provider with fully independent intellectual property. Its industrial continuous pyrolysis equipment (10,000–50,000 tpy per unit) handles more than 30 waste types including scrap tires, waste plastics, oily sludge, tar residue and medical waste. Niutech has delivered 10,000-tpy-class projects across dozens of countries including Germany, the UK, South Korea, Denmark and Brazil.

text:
Investors tracking Thyssenkrupp's long-running transformation story have a fresh stack of catalysts to digest. The German industrial group is pressing ahead with its plan to dismantle its conglomerate structure, and the details emerging this week paint a picture of a company in motion — even if one of its green-energy units continues to cast a shadow.

Materials Services Gets a Name and a Structure

The most significant development came on Wednesday, when management unveiled the blueprint for spinning off its Materials Services division. The unit will operate under the new name "tk accelis," with Thyssenkrupp planning to distribute 49 percent of the shares to existing shareholders via a listing on the Frankfurt exchange before the year is out. The parent will retain a controlling 51 percent stake.

The move is the latest in a series of structural measures aimed at giving individual business units greater independence on the capital markets. It follows the separate listing of the naval division TKMS, in which the group also holds a 51 percent stake — a structure that is becoming something of a template for the group's divestment strategy.

Naval Division Delivers on Multiple Fronts

The defence arm, in particular, is providing the kind of momentum that restructuring stories thrive on. TKMS reported an order backlog of €20.1 billion for the first nine months of the fiscal year, with adjusted EBIT of €131 million. Management has indicated that figure could climb above €25 billion once an anticipated frigate programme is factored in.

That pipeline is being actively replenished. On the same day as the spin-off announcement, TKMS confirmed two notable advances: it has emerged as the preferred supplier for Canada's submarine programme, a project that could involve up to twelve 212CD-class vessels, and it has signed a contract with the German Navy for four MEKO A-200 DEU frigates.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Thyssenkrupp?

For holders of the parent company's stock, the rising value of the TKMS stake adds another layer to the turnaround narrative — one that operates independently of the traditional steel business.

Steel and Green Investments Move Forward

Away from the headlines, operational progress continues. The Rasselstein subsidiary has announced plans to install an 8-megawatt ground-mounted solar array at its Andernach site, with commissioning targeted for mid-2027. The project is designed to decarbonise tinplate production — a modest but symbolic step toward the climate-neutral steelmaking that has become a central strategic theme.

In Duisburg, meanwhile, Thyssenkrupp Steel has granted final acceptance to Primetals Technologies for a new continuous caster, designated No. 4. The facility is geared toward high-margin premium steel grades, marking a concrete advance in the shift toward higher-value products. The group is also expanding hydrogen infrastructure for its Nucera subsidiary under the Carbon2Chem research project and planning a facility for sustainable aviation fuel production.

Nucera Remains the Weak Link

Not every division is firing on all cylinders. Thyssenkrupp Nucera, the electrolyser specialist, saw order intake slump to just €81 million in the third quarter. The company responded by trimming the top end of its full-year order intake guidance for the period ending September 2026, from €850 million to €670 million, and slashed its revenue expectation for the green hydrogen segment to a range of €100 million to €130 million.

Berenberg analysts responded on August 25 by cutting their revenue and earnings forecasts for the 2026 through 2028 fiscal years, though they maintained a "Hold" rating on the stock.

Shares Near Multi-Year Highs

The market's verdict on the broader story remains emphatically positive. Thyssenkrupp shares closed Friday at €14.67, down 1.2 percent on the day but up 9.2 percent on the week. Over the past 30 days, the stock has gained 23 percent, and it now sits just 3.4 percent below its 52-week high of €15.18, reached in late August. Year-to-date, the shares are up 57 percent.

Thyssenkrupp at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

The rally has drawn fresh support from the analyst community. DZ Bank upgraded the stock from "Hold" to "Buy" on August 21, while Bank of America reaffirmed its "Buy" rating on August 20 and lifted its price target from €19.00 to €22.00.

What's Next on the Calendar

Investors have two key dates on the horizon. Management is planning a capital markets day focused on the Steel Europe division in London at the end of September, though an exact date has yet to be confirmed. Then, on December 8, the group will publish its full-year results for fiscal 2025/2026.

There is also a structural milestone to watch: the twelve-month lock-up period on Thyssenkrupp's 51 percent stake in TKMS expires in October 2026, a moment that could theoretically open the door to changes in the ownership structure of the naval unit.

For now, the combination of a well-filled defence order book, tangible progress in the steel business, and a steady stream of green investment commitments is keeping the transformation story firmly on track — even as Nucera's struggles serve as a reminder that not every chapter of this restructuring will be smooth.

title: Europe's Airfares Swing Sharply in 2026 as Demand Growth Reshapes Travel Costs
description:
I see that European airfares swings matter because passenger demand remains strong while airport capacity, fuel transition costs and seasonal pressure continue shaping airline pricing.
At the beginning of 2026, prices declined year on year.
Strong Passenger Demand Continues to Shape Prices The latest complete annual passenger figures available before the specified verification date show that demand remained powerful.
Environmental Efficiency Is Improving The 2025 European Aviation Environmental Report provides a broader assessment of the sector’s performance.
European Price Transparency Rules Matter to Travellers A low advertised fare does not always represent the final amount paid.
text:
European airfares are moving through a volatile period creating sharp differences in travel costs across months and markets. Eurostat recorded EU air-transport prices falling 4.7% year on year in April 2026 before rising 8.1% in May and 3.1% in June. I see that European airfares swings matter because passenger demand remains strong while airport capacity, fuel transition costs and seasonal pressure continue shaping airline pricing. Official evidence therefore rejects any claim that one carrier is always Europe’s cheapest or costliest. Travellers, tourism businesses and destinations must instead examine routes, dates, fare conditions and the full booking price before drawing conclusions, about airfares with confidence.

European Airfares Defy a Simple Cheapest Airline Ranking

Attempts to identify Europe’s cheapest or most expensive airline often reduce a complicated market to a single headline. Official evidence shows why that approach can mislead travellers. European airfares change according to routes, travel dates, booking times, cabin classes, demand patterns, airport charges and the optional services selected by customers.

Revenue per available seat kilometre, commonly known as RASK, is sometimes used to rank airlines by supposed affordability. However, it is an airline revenue metric rather than a direct measurement of the ticket price paid by an individual passenger. It can incorporate passenger revenue collected across different routes, cabins and market conditions.

A regional airline serving remote communities may record high revenue per seat kilometre because it operates short sectors with limited capacity and relatively high operating costs. That does not automatically establish that it sells Europe’s most expensive tickets across comparable journeys.

Likewise, a large low-cost operator can record a relatively low RASK while charging different prices for the same route depending on demand, booking time and remaining capacity. Travellers may also pay separately for baggage, preferred seating, priority boarding, airport check-in or ticket flexibility.

Eurostat’s Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices offers a more appropriate official measure of how household prices change over time. Even that index measures price movement, not which airline offers the lowest fare on every route. The evidence therefore supports analysis of trends rather than a permanent airline league table.

European Airfares Recorded Dramatic Monthly Reversals

The most important official development available by 4 August 2026 came from Eurostat’s analysis of air-transport prices between January 2025 and June 2026.

EU air-transport service prices increased by 13.7% in April 2025 compared with April 2024. Growth became more moderate during the subsequent summer months before another period of sharp movement emerged in 2026.

At the beginning of 2026, prices declined year on year. They subsequently increased during February and March before falling by 4.7% in April. That fall was immediately followed by an 8.1% annual increase in May and a 3.1% rise in June.

The sequence is significant. It shows that flight prices in Europe can move from annual decline to substantial growth in only one month. It also demonstrates why a fare observed during one booking period cannot reliably define the affordability of an airline throughout the year.

International aviation produced particularly strong variations. Eurostat reported that international air-travel prices increased by 8.7% year on year in May 2026 and 4.5% in June. Domestic air travel recorded a smaller 2% annual increase in June.

These figures indicate that international services exerted a stronger influence on the overall movement in air-transport prices. They do not, however, show that every passenger paid 4.5% more. Harmonised inflation figures track average price changes across a representative collection of services rather than identical outcomes for every itinerary.

Eurostat’s findings provide the clearest official basis for reporting the 2026 trend: airfare inflation was not travelling in one direction. It was fluctuating sharply. Eurostat’s official airfare analysis was published on 23 July 2026.

National Markets Moved in Radically Different Directions

Europe’s headline airfare movement concealed dramatic differences between EU countries. These variations further undermine claims that the continent has one uniform pricing environment.

Belgium recorded annual air-transport price increases of 41.5% in April 2026, 33.8% in May and 28.7% in June. Slovakia moved in the opposite direction, with decreases of 53% in April, 48.2% in May and 45.1% in June.

Austria registered a 22.3% annual increase in June, while Greece recorded growth of 15.1%. Hungary and Poland reported decreases of 13.6% and 13.1% respectively.

Such figures should be interpreted carefully. They describe changes from the corresponding month of the previous year. They do not establish that Belgium had Europe’s highest average ticket price or that Slovakia sold its cheapest flights.

A market showing a large annual decrease may be comparing current prices with an unusually expensive period a year earlier. A substantial increase can similarly reflect a low comparison base, changing route supply, different seasonal timing or altered demand.

National inflation rates can also be influenced by the composition of flights purchased by consumers. Countries with different balances of domestic, intra-European and long-haul travel will not necessarily follow the same price pattern.

The data nevertheless carry an important message for destinations and travel businesses. The affordability of reaching one European country may change very differently from another, even during the same month. Tour operators and destination marketers cannot safely apply an EU-wide price assumption to each source market.

Why Airline Revenue Is Not the Same as a Passenger Fare

Understanding the difference between revenue performance and consumer pricing is essential when interpreting airline comparisons.

Available seat kilometres measure an airline’s passenger-carrying capacity by multiplying the seats available by the distance flown. RASK then relates revenue to that capacity. It is useful for analysing airline economics, but it does not reproduce the price shown to a traveller during a booking search.

Several factors explain the distinction:

Airlines sell multiple cabins and fare classes.

Prices change as departure approaches and seats are sold.

Route lengths differ substantially.

Connecting journeys cannot be compared directly with nonstop sectors.

Ancillary services may be included or charged separately.

Loyalty redemptions and corporate agreements affect revenue.

Regional public-service routes operate under different conditions.

Network airlines carry connecting passengers through hubs.

Seasonal operators may concentrate capacity within limited periods.

A carrier operating short regional flights can generate high revenue per available seat kilometre because fixed expenses are spread across fewer kilometres. Airports serving remote areas may also lack the passenger volumes available at major hubs.

By contrast, an airline operating longer sectors produces many more seat kilometres on each flight. Its RASK may therefore be lower even when the total fare paid for an individual journey is higher.

Official price indices answer a different question: how much have prices paid by households changed? Neither measurement can identify a universally cheapest airline without a carefully controlled comparison involving the same route, date, booking window, fare inclusions and service conditions.

Strong Passenger Demand Continues to Shape Prices

The latest complete annual passenger figures available before the specified verification date show that demand remained powerful.

Eurostat reported 1.1 billion air passengers in the EU during 2024, representing an 8.3% increase from 973 million in 2023. Passenger numbers also moved above the one-billion level recorded in 2019, before the pandemic disrupted international aviation.

Every EU country recorded annual passenger growth in 2024. Hungary registered the strongest rise at 19.2%, followed by Czechia at 18.9% and Estonia at 17.8%. Sweden recorded the smallest increase at 1.3%, while Bulgaria grew by 3.8%. France and Ireland each increased by 4.6%.

Monthly EU passenger totals increased throughout 2024 compared with the corresponding periods of 2023. February produced the fastest growth at 13%, followed by March at 12.1% and May at 10%.

The expansion was also visible in intra-EU travel. Spain handled 123.8 million intra-EU passengers during 2024, the highest total among member countries. Hungary’s intra-EU passenger traffic increased by 22.1% to 11.3 million.

This broad-based recovery matters for European airfares because strong demand can support higher pricing on constrained routes. Yet the relationship is not automatic. Airlines may add capacity, competitors may enter a market, or travellers may switch destinations when fares become unattractive.

The effect therefore depends on whether seat supply grows fast enough to meet demand in each market. Eurostat’s official air-passenger statistics provide the relevant annual evidence.

Flight Capacity Has Recovered but Constraints Remain

Commercial flight numbers provide a second measure of the recovery. Eurostat recorded 6.7 million commercial flights in the EU during 2024, an increase of 5.8% from 6.3 million in 2023.

However, the total remained below the seven million commercial flights recorded in 2019. Passenger numbers had already exceeded their pre-pandemic level, while flight movements had not fully recovered.

That difference suggests the aviation system was carrying more passengers with fewer flights than in 2019. Larger aircraft, stronger load factors and changing airline networks can all contribute to this outcome.

Greater efficiency can help airlines spread operating costs over more passengers. However, fuller aircraft can also leave fewer discounted seats available on high-demand departures. Capacity recovery therefore does not guarantee uniformly lower fares.

Airport infrastructure also limits how quickly supply can expand. Slot-constrained hubs cannot simply add unlimited departures when demand rises. Air-traffic-management capacity, staffing, runway availability and terminal limitations can influence schedules.

EUROCONTROL expected European traffic during summer 2026 to grow by an average of 2% compared with summer 2025. In some weeks, traffic could rise by as much as 5.1%. The organisation warned that the network was already saturated and required close coordination to use available capacity effectively.

This forecast matters because congestion can create operational costs and reduce schedule resilience. Delays may increase aircraft, crew and passenger-care expenses. Airlines then face commercial decisions about whether those pressures can be absorbed or reflected in prices.

Euro control’s summer 2026 assessment supports the conclusion that rising demand is meeting an increasingly busy network.

Europe Returned to Pre-Pandemic Traffic Volumes

Euro control’s spring 2026 forecast placed the wider European recovery in a longer-term context.

Europe recorded approximately 11.05 million flights in 2025, averaging 30,263 flights each day. That represented growth of 4% over 2024 and brought traffic back to 100% of its 2019 level.

Southern and eastern Europe performed more strongly than previously expected, while traffic extending beyond the European Civil Aviation Conference area also remained robust.

By early July 2026, EUROCONTROL recorded an average of 36,055 daily flights across its network during the week from 29 June to 5 July. That was 1.4% higher than the preceding week and 3.4% above the corresponding period in 2025.

These flight totals are broader than Eurostat’s EU-only figures because EUROCONTROL monitors a wider European aviation network. They should not be combined as if they covered an identical geography.

Together, however, the two official datasets establish that European aviation had moved beyond its initial recovery phase. The industry was managing mature demand at or near pre-pandemic traffic levels.

That transition has pricing implications. During the early recovery, airlines could reopen dormant capacity and restore suspended routes. Once traffic returns to earlier levels, further expansion may depend more heavily on aircraft availability, airport capacity, airspace performance and infrastructure investment.

International Disruption Can Change Capacity Quickly

European pricing cannot be separated from geopolitical and operational conditions outside the continent.

EUROCONTROL recorded 30,236 daily flights during the week of 6–12 April 2026. That was 2% below the corresponding week of 2025. Traffic flows increased in most regions, but services between Europe and the Middle East were down by 54%.

By the week of 29 June–5 July, Europe–Middle East flights had increased by 13% from the previous week and stood 3% above 2025 levels.

These official snapshots demonstrate how quickly international capacity can contract and recover. They do not prove a specific effect on individual fares, but changes of this scale can alter available seats, connecting opportunities and route competition.

When airspace restrictions require longer routings, airlines may consume more fuel and crew time. The services are cancelled, displaced demand can move towards remaining flights. When operations recover, additional capacity can relieve pressure.

For travellers, the practical lesson is that route-specific conditions matter more than a continent-wide airline label. A carrier offering strong value on one market may face a completely different operating environment elsewhere.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Introduces a New Cost Variable

European aviation entered a new regulatory phase in 2025 when the ReFuelEU Aviation requirement began applying a minimum sustainable aviation fuel share at designated EU airports.

The regulation established a 2% sustainable aviation fuel requirement from 2025. The proportion is scheduled to rise progressively, reaching 70% by 2050. The framework is intended to reduce aviation’s dependence on fossil fuel and lower lifecycle emissions.

EASA’s first ReFuelEU technical report found that sustainable aviation fuel represented 0.6% of reported aviation fuel supplied at EU airports in 2024, equivalent to approximately 193 kilo tonnes. It was supplied at 33 EU airports across 12 member states.

Reported sustainable fuel achieved an average lifecycle emissions reduction of around 91% and avoided an estimated 714 kilo tonnes of carbon-dioxide-equivalent emissions.

However, the official report also identified a major price difference. Average sustainable aviation fuel cost €2,085 per tonne in 2024, compared with €734 per tonne for conventional jet fuel. That made the reported average sustainable product almost three times as expensive.

The comparison does not mean fares will rise by the same proportion. Fuel represents only one component of airline expenditure, and carriers make different commercial decisions about efficiency, hedging, pricing and cost recovery.

It does demonstrate that the environmental transition introduces a material cost pressure. Increasing supply, supporting production and developing synthetic fuels will be important if Europe is to meet higher mandates without creating unnecessary market disruption.

EASA’s ReFuelEU Aviation report supplies the official fuel and price evidence.

Environmental Efficiency Is Improving

The 2025 European Aviation Environmental Report provides a broader assessment of the sector’s performance.

Flights departing EU and European Free Trade Association airports emitted 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2023. This was 10% below the corresponding level in 2019.

Average carbon-dioxide emissions per passenger kilometre declined to 83 grams in 2023, equivalent to approximately 3.3 litres of fuel per 100 passenger kilometres.

Single-aisle and twin-aisle jets accounted for 77% of departures and 96% of carbon-dioxide emissions. Long-haul flights covering more than 4,000 kilometres represented only 6% of flights but produced 46% of emissions.

These statistics show why ticket prices cannot be understood solely through competition and demand. European policy is increasingly designed to change the fuels, technology and operating practices used by airlines.

Newer aircraft, stronger load factors and more efficient operations can reduce emissions intensity and fuel consumption. Nevertheless, growing traffic can offset some efficiency gains at system level.

EASA’s traffic scenarios also show considerable uncertainty. Under its higher-growth scenario, flights could grow by 1.6% annually and passenger kilometres by 1.8% between 2025 and 2050. Under the low scenario, flight growth could remain close to zero until 2045.

The range reflects uncertainty involving energy prices, economic conditions, capacity and policy. It also reinforces why long-term airfare predictions should be treated cautiously.

EASA’s official environmental report provides the emissions and efficiency figures.

European Price Transparency Rules Matter to Travellers

A low advertised fare does not always represent the final amount paid. EU law consequently requires specific pricing information to be shown to consumers.

Under the EU Air Services Regulation, the final price must be indicated and must include the applicable air fare or air rate as well as unavoidable and foreseeable taxes, charges, surcharges and fees.

Optional price supplements must be communicated clearly, transparently and unambiguously at the beginning of the booking process. Consumers must actively choose optional services rather than have them imposed through pres elected choices.

These rules help travellers compare offers, but comparison still requires attention. Baggage allowances, seat-selection policies, flexibility and airport locations can differ even when initial prices appear similar.

A flight into a secondary airport may have a lower headline fare but generate higher surface-transport costs. A restrictive ticket may become expensive if plans change. A fare including checked baggage may offer better total value than a cheaper basic ticket once additional services are purchased.

The European Commission began consulting on revisions to the Air Services Regulation in 2025. The framework governs access to the EU aviation market and includes rules about the presentation of ticket prices.

For travel publishers, accurate reporting should therefore distinguish among:

Advertised base fares

Mandatory taxes and fees

Optional ancillary services

Total journey costs

Airline revenue metrics

Official consumer-price indices

Collapsing these categories into one “cheapest airline” claim risks presenting unlike measurements as though they were interchangeable.

The European Commission’s Air Services Regulation review explains the role of the framework.

Air-Passenger Rights Can Affect the Real Value of a Fare

Price is only one element of travel value. Passenger protection becomes particularly important when flights are cancelled, heavily delayed or overbooked.

EU air-passenger rights may provide assistance, reimbursement, rerouting or compensation depending on the journey, disruption and circumstances. The applicable rules depend on factors including departure location, carrier status and the cause of the disruption.

A cheaper fare is not necessarily better value if its schedule, airport, connection risk or flexibility creates additional costs.

Airline punctuality, schedule frequency and available alternatives can also influence the practical value of a ticket. A route served several times daily may provide more recovery options than an infrequent regional service.

This is particularly relevant when comparing network, regional and low-cost airlines. Each model serves different travel needs and distributes costs differently.

Tourism Destinations Face Uneven Effects

Airfare volatility can influence where visitors travel, how long they stay and when they book. Islands and geographically peripheral markets often have fewer practical alternatives to air travel.

Eurostat found that aircraft accounted for 14.7% of EU passenger kilometres in 2023, up 1.6 percentage points from 2022. Croatia recorded the highest national share of air passenger kilometres within total transport performance at 43.5%, followed by Bulgaria at 29% and Cyprus at 27.4%.

The figures do not measure tourism alone, but they illustrate the importance of aviation to mobility in several destination economies.

When fares rise sharply in a source market, travellers may shorten visits, change dates or select alternative destinations. Conversely, falling fares or new capacity can expand demand and distribute visitors beyond established gateways. Tourism boards must consequently monitor route-level accessibility rather than rely only on total national arrivals.

Businesses Must Manage Pricing Volatility

Tour operators, travel-management companies and hospitality businesses face their own consequences from unstable airfare patterns.

Package prices can become harder to maintain when flight costs move sharply between months.

Businesses can respond through flexible travel windows, earlier booking, alternative airports and clearer communication about fare inclusions. However, there is no universal strategy. Booking early does not guarantee the lowest price, while waiting can expose customers to reduced availability.

Official price data are most useful for understanding market direction, not predicting an individual fare. Travel sellers still require live booking information for commercial decisions.

Destination businesses should also avoid interpreting national airfare inflation as a direct forecast of visitor numbers. Demand depends on household income, exchange rates, accommodation costs, consumer confidence and competing destinations as well as flights.

What Travellers Should Compare Before Booking

Travellers seeking lower costs should compare the complete journey rather than selecting an airline from a general ranking.

The most useful checks include:

The final price after unavoidable charges

Cabin and checked-baggage allowances

Seat-selection costs

Airport location and ground transport

Departure and arrival times

Connection length and protection

Ticket-change conditions

Cancellation and refund terms

Passport, visa and entry requirements

Passenger rights applying to the itinerary

Price comparisons should use the same dates, routes, baggage requirements and fare conditions. Otherwise, one offer may appear cheaper simply because it includes less.

Flexible-date searches can reveal substantial variations around weekends, holidays and major events. Travellers should also check whether a connection requires baggage collection or a terminal transfer.

The key principle is straightforward: European airfares are dynamic products. Neither an annual revenue metric nor one sample booking can define a carrier’s affordability across an entire continent.

Outlook for European Airfares Beyond 2026

The official outlook suggests continued demand growth but substantial uncertainty.

Euro control’s spring forecast projected European flight growth through 2032, while EASA’s longer-term scenarios presented a wide range of possible outcomes. Airport capacity, economic performance, geopolitical disruption and fuel prices remain important variables.

Sustainable aviation requirements will become progressively stronger.

At the same time, aircraft technology, operational efficiency and expanding sustainable-fuel production may reduce some cost pressure. Competition can also constrain fares when multiple carriers offer capacity on the same route.

Eurostat’s 2026 data already showed annual declines followed by rapid increases within successive months.

The most defensible conclusion is that European flight pricing will remain dynamic and uneven. Travellers will continue to encounter attractive fares, but availability will vary across dates, airports and routes.

Conclusion

As a travelers I find it hard to rely on a list that says which airline is always the cheapest or the most expensive. European airfares in 2026 cannot be reduced to such a list. Eurostat recorded reversals in air-transport inflation and huge differences between national markets. Meanwhile passenger demand, infrastructure, international disruption and the need for sustainable fuel keep shaping airline economics. RASK may shed light on airline revenue performance. Rask does not show the fare paid for a comparable journey. Travellers should look at prices, baggage fees, flexibility, airports and journey conditions before booking. For tourism businesses and destinations official evidence points to continued aviation growth with volatile costs, uneven accessibility and growing environmental obligations, across Europe’s travel market.

text:
Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) plans to increase the refining capacity of its Kochi Refinery in Kerala from 15.5 million metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) to 17 MTPA.

The proposed expansion is aimed at improving operational flexibility and enabling BPCL to respond to rising energy demand. It will also support closer integration between the company’s refining and petrochemical operations.

BPCL Chairman and Managing Director Sanjay Khanna said the capacity increase, along with the ongoing polypropylene project at Kochi, will help the company expand its portfolio of higher-value products.

The proposed increase comes as BPCL’s refining operations recorded higher throughput. Its refineries processed a record 41.2 million tonnes of crude during FY2025-26, reflecting continued demand for refining capacity.

Refining and petrochemicals move closer

BPCL is also progressing with an integrated refinery expansion and petrochemical project at its Bina Refinery in Madhya Pradesh.

The Bina project is expected to be supported by downstream petrochemical units, with the planned facilities aimed at creating an integrated energy and petrochemical complex in Central India. The development is part of BPCL’s broader strategy to increase petrochemical integration alongside its refining operations.

At Kochi, the proposed capacity increase and polypropylene project are expected to strengthen the refinery’s ability to support downstream product manufacturing. Greater integration between refining and petrochemicals can also enable refiners to move towards products with higher value addition.

BPCL expands refining and product portfolio

The Kochi expansion and Bina development form part of BPCL’s efforts to strengthen its refining network while increasing its presence in petrochemicals.

The increase in Kochi’s capacity to 17 MTPA would add further processing capability to BPCL’s existing refinery network. Combined with the company’s investments in petrochemical units, the projects are expected to support a more integrated refining and downstream manufacturing model.

The focus on refining capacity and petrochemical integration comes as India’s energy demand continues to grow and refiners seek to increase the share of higher-value products in their portfolios.

text:
SandboxAQ delivered a busy week of product expansion and research updates, underscoring its push to commercialize physics‑grounded AI across healthcare, life sciences, materials, and enterprise productivity. The privately held firm advanced both its Large Quantitative Models and workflow tools, while highlighting growing exposure to regulated and industrial markets.

In healthcare, SandboxAQ’s AQMed unit showcased the investigational CardiAQ magnetocardiography system for triaging U.S. emergency‑department chest‑pain patients. The five‑minute, non‑invasive scan aims to detect ischemic signals that standard ECGs may miss, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy but still facing clinical, regulatory, and reimbursement hurdles.

The company also broadened its footprint in enterprise AI with the launch of Switch, an open‑source orchestration layer for embedding AI agents directly into Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, and similar tools. Switch, part of the Flint AI portfolio, is designed to be model‑ and platform‑agnostic, reducing vendor lock‑in and turning chat channels into persistent rooms where humans and multiple agents share context.

Switch’s free Apache 2.0 with Commons Clause license positions it as a developer‑friendly entry point that could later drive demand for paid support and integration services. By dogfooding Switch internally and emphasizing secure, reusable, and auditable contexts, SandboxAQ is targeting enterprises that want to scale multi‑agent workflows without overhauling existing communication stacks.

In drug discovery, SandboxAQ reported that its AQPotency model is now generally available on Anthropic’s Claude platform for natural‑language, no‑code binding‑strength prediction. The tool claims docking‑like performance while rapidly scoring thousands of protein–ligand pairs, with transparency features such as applicability scores and uncertainty estimates aimed at risk‑averse pharma customers.

The company further highlighted PD‑KG, a large knowledge graph integrating multi‑omics and clinical data to prioritize Parkinson’s disease targets, and its scientific presence at the ACS Fall 2026 meeting. Presentations on machine‑learning force fields and deep‑learning co‑folding models support its positioning at the intersection of high‑rigor physics and scalable drug discovery workflows.

In materials and energy, SandboxAQ continued to promote AQCat, its catalyst discovery model, now generally available on both AWS Marketplace and Anthropic’s Claude. Trained on 13.5 million quantum‑chemistry calculations, AQCat targets decarbonization‑related applications such as green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuel, fertilizers, and plastics recycling by delivering near‑DFT accuracy at dramatically higher speeds.

The company also showcased AI tools for discovering PFAS‑free materials for semiconductor manufacturing, leveraging Large Quantitative Models and generative AI to virtually screen candidates before synthesis. These efforts could help chipmakers respond to tightening environmental rules while expanding SandboxAQ’s addressable market in advanced materials.

A broader theme of workflow integration emerged as SandboxAQ promoted AI‑driven orchestration with Flint AI’s Switch and emphasized flexible deployment across Claude, AWS, and existing enterprise stacks. This multi‑channel strategy is aimed at lowering adoption barriers, moving from bespoke engagements to recurring, subscription‑like usage in industrial and scientific R&D.

Overall, the week underscored SandboxAQ’s strategy of combining physics‑aware AI models with practical deployment paths in healthcare, life sciences, energy, and enterprise productivity. While many offerings remain early‑stage or investigational, their expansion into major cloud and AI platforms, along with scientific visibility, could enhance the company’s long‑term commercial prospects if customer adoption scales.

GeoPura is providing green hydrogen power for Lorde’s FORWARDS Presents concert and FORWARDS Festival on Clifton Downs, Bristol, as part of a major clean power pilot replacing diesel generation at live events.

GeoPura’s Hydrogen Power Units (HPUs) and green hydrogen will provide critical power for the main stage across Lorde’s one-off concert on Friday 28 August and FORWARDS Festival on 29-30 August, where artists including Little Simz, Tems and Goldie will perform.

The deployment forms part of the West of England Clean Power Pilot, which is testing how green hydrogen and battery systems can replace diesel generators across Bristol’s live music, film and TV sectors. The initiative builds on the legacy of Massive Attack’s ACT 1.5 show on Bristol Downs in 2024.

GeoPura’s HPUs generate electricity from green hydrogen with no CO2, NOx or particulate emissions at the point of use, with pure water as the only by-product. Artists performing on FORWARDS’ West Stage will even be invited to drink the water produced from the generation of power for their performances.

Camilla Carson, Chief Commercial Officer at GeoPura, said: “Major events need significant amounts of reliable power, but that shouldn’t come at the expense of the environment, or the air people breathe. The West of England Clean Power Pilot is showing what can be achieved when industry comes together to move away from fossil fuel generation.

“We’re excited to support Lorde and FORWARDS with clean power generation using our Hydrogen Power Units and green hydrogen, delivering the critical power needed for the main stage with no CO2, NOx or particulate emissions. It means cleaner air for artists, crews and audiences, with water as the only by-product of generating power.

“This is proven technology delivering at scale today, ready to support live events, film and TV and many other sectors.”

text:
Burdened by rising fuel import costs and an "ocean crisis" of record-breaking heat, Pacific island nations are seeking to build support for a new regional fund ahead of COP31, intended to channel investment into renewable energy, community resilience and ocean protection, experts said.

Leaders from the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), including Australia and New Zealand, are expected to issue a call for global pledges to the Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF) at a high-level meeting this coming week in Palau, seeking to build a new model for financing climate action.

The new regional fund was formally launched in May this year and is meant to "serve communities at a community level", swiftly channelling investments for their projects on the ground, according to Fiji's assistant minister for foreign affairs, Lenora Qereqeretabua.

"We are expecting pledges for the PRF, and these funds will go to communities that apply," she told journalists at an online briefing. "We have organised it in such a way that it makes our application processes much, much easier than applying for global funding."

Qereqeretabua added that she expects that PRF funds will be "utilised by communities to protect themselves from climate change and the effects of climate change."

The Pacific Islands Forum meeting is expected to shape the region's priorities ahead of this year's pre-COP, hosted by Fiji and Tuvalu, and COP31, which will be co-led by Australia and Türkiye.

At COP31, a dedicated session on the climate finance needs of small island states will seek to drive pledges into the PRF. The fund has so far received about $172 million in capital – with about $67 million coming from Australia – and aims to close the year with $500 million.

Ocean heat and fossil fuel shocks

Leaders from the Pacific will meet in Palau from Sunday amid an "ocean crisis" of record-breaking ocean heat caused by this year's "super El Niño", according to Kevin Chand, Pacific ocean policy director at National Geographic's Pristine Seas conservation project.

Leaders at the PIF are expected to put forward commitments towards new marine protected areas, which will be key for shielding ecosystems from future climate extremes, Chand said. The forum is expected to issue a statement on the need for ocean action at COP31, and announce commitments towards reaching the global goal of protecting 30% of the planet's land and sea ecosystems by 2030.

Rising ocean heat could lead to food insecurity and lost government earnings in the region, as key fish stocks like tuna start migrating away from their coastline in search of colder waters, said Coral Pasisi, director of climate change and sustainability at the Pacific Community (SPC).

Climate shocks are deepening existing economic pressures, as Pacific nations have spent up to a quarter of their GDP on fossil fuel imports due to the war in Iran, according to a recent report by the University of New South Wales (UNSW) in Australia.

Wesley Morgan, one of the study's authors, told journalists that partner nations "ought to be putting their money where their mouth is", and should support the energy transition in the Pacific by covering the upfront costs of switching from polluting diesel to solar power, batteries and electricity grid upgrades.

China keeps Indonesia’s battery dream afloat but future less certain

Given the increase in climate-related shocks and sea-level rise, the PIF should also mention the need to phase out fossil fuel extraction and consumption, said Sindra Sharma, international policy lead at the Pacific Islands Climate Action Network (PICAN).

Last year's COP30 failed to deliver a global roadmap on transitioning away from fossil fuels, which led to a group of countries – including several Pacific island nations – pursuing their own fossil fuel phase-out summit in Santa Marta, Colombia. Next year's conference will be hosted by Tuvalu and co-chaired by Ireland, which should also receive backing from the PIF, Sharma said.

Both the chairs of the Santa Marta coalition and the Australian COP31 co-presidency have vowed to continue a push for this topic to be discussed at COP31.

New fund to test allies

As local communities in the Pacific struggle to access global climate funds, the PRF's planned model for quick, direct disbursements has "very solid and good" intentions, Sharma said, but it will need political and financial backing from donor countries.

"The proof is going to be when the fund actually starts operating and delivering to communities," she added. "If there is too much bureaucracy in being able to access the funds, for example. These things will have to be scrutinised."

The facility aims to deliver funds in two categories: one for climate adaptation and "disaster resilience", and another for social and community resilience that includes areas like community capacity-building, education, data analytics and financial management, among others. It will launch its first call for proposals at the PIF.

Morgan added that Australia will need to "leverage global interests" so that funding is directed to the Pacific Resilience Facility "or else the Pacific won't be able to trust Australia as a partner". The country ratified the PRF treaty in May, triggering its entry into force.

"The perception [of Australia] in the region is genuinely divided, and it's worth being honest about it," Sharma said, adding that the pre-COP31 in Fiji, which is usually limited to a technical space for negotiations, will determine how meaningful Australia's advocacy for the Pacific can be.

This time, Pacific nations want to use the pre-COP in early October as an opportunity to demonstrate the challenges their largely low-lying islands face and to advocate for their political priorities, including a renewed global effort to limit global warming to 1.5C by cutting emissions faster and deeper. World leaders are due to visit Tuvalu to experience the frontline of rising sea levels, although Australia and Fiji have yet to confirm who will attend.

"In Bonn, Australia was largely missing on the negotiated outcomes that we so urgently need to see. It's not enough to get Pacific priorities on the agenda. Agenda placement is not delivery," Sharma added.

text:
Neste stock (FI0009013296) is trading in the low-teen euro range on the Helsinki exchange as investors digest a consensus view that pairs strong current-year growth expectations with forecasts for a notable earnings decline next year as of August 28, 2026.

The latest market snapshot shows Neste quoted near EUR 13.07 on the Helsinki market, giving retail investors a clear sense of where the shares currently sit versus recent levels as of late August 2026.

Against this price backdrop, the most recent analyst overview indicates that the company is expected to deliver a substantial 327.88 percent increase in earnings for the current year 2026, followed by a projected 25.82 percent decline in earnings for 2027, highlighting how volatile the profit trajectory is expected to be over the coming two-year period.

These consensus figures underscore that the current year is seen as a recovery phase after weaker results, with a very strong rebound baked into forecasts, while the following year is modeled as a normalization period in which earnings pull back from temporarily elevated levels.

Recent market data for Neste

Market data compiled for the Helsinki listing shows Neste shares quoted at EUR 13.07, positioning the stock in a relatively tight trading band in late August 2026, even as sector peers experience more pronounced swings.

At this level, the stock price suggests that the market is not pricing in dramatic short-term changes, which can matter for retail investors who are watching for either breakouts or sharp corrections when deciding on entry and exit points.

If the share price were to move significantly higher from EUR 13.07 in the coming sessions while earnings expectations remained unchanged, valuation multiples would expand, whereas a drop below this level without a change in forecasts would compress multiples and potentially improve the implied earnings yield.

For now, the low-teen euro trading zone marks a reference point that investors can use to compare the current valuation with historical ranges once more detailed price history or 52-week high and low figures are available.

Consensus points to sharp earnings swings

The current consensus overview for Neste highlights unusually large percentage changes in earnings expectations across reporting periods, with the current quarter, the next quarter, the current year and the next year all showing double- and triple-digit percentage swings.

In the present quarter, the expected earnings change of 230.63 percent compared with the prior-year quarter suggests that analysts anticipate a significant improvement in profitability within the short term, which is a striking number even in cyclical industries.

For the next quarter, the projected earnings change of 26.00 percent indicates a more moderate, but still meaningful, increase relative to the comparable period, implying that the strong momentum seen in the current quarter may carry over but at a less dramatic pace.

The most eye-catching figure is the 327.88 percent expected change in earnings for the full current year 2026, which effectively signals that analysts foresee more than a tripling of profitability versus the previous year, a pattern often associated with recovery from a depressed base or the realization of major strategic initiatives.

In stark contrast, the forecast for the next year 2027 shows a negative 25.82 percent change in earnings compared with 2026, meaning that after the very strong rebound in the current year, profits are expected to decline by about one quarter, though from a much higher level than in the prior downturn period.

For investors, this quantified comparison matters because it frames 2026 as a peak or catch-up year in the consensus models, while 2027 is treated as a step down toward more sustainable long-run earnings power rather than a continuation of the outsized growth rates.

The combination of a 327.88 percent jump followed by a 25.82 percent drop also suggests that analysts see a relatively narrow window for exceptionally strong profits, making timing and valuation considerations more important for those choosing when to engage with the stock.

If the actual reported earnings for 2026 come in significantly above the projected 327.88 percent increase, the subsequent 2027 decline could prove less severe in percentage terms, whereas a miss relative to this aggressive growth expectation might prompt further downward revisions for 2027.

Such large swings in forward-looking metrics often reflect both changing macro conditions and company-specific factors, including feedstock costs, margins in renewable products and refining, and the pace at which new capacity and projects contribute to the bottom line.

How consensus shapes the investor view

For retail investors evaluating Neste stock, the contrast between a relatively unremarkable current share price around EUR 13.07 and the dramatic forecasted changes in earnings can create a nuanced picture, especially when compared with more stable peers.

On one hand, a 327.88 percent jump in expected current-year earnings means that the forward price-to-earnings ratio based on 2026 forecasts may be far lower than what backward-looking figures suggest, potentially making the stock appear inexpensive relative to earnings power if the rebound materializes as modeled.

On the other hand, the 25.82 percent anticipated decline in 2027 earnings implies that using 2026 as a baseline could overstate long-term profitability and understate risk, since the elevated earnings might not be sustained beyond the current high point.

These dynamics make it important for investors to examine how consensus evolves over time, watching for revisions after each quarterly report, which can either smooth out the projected volatility or reinforce the view that the business is entering a more cyclical phase.

For example, if after the next earnings release the 2026 forecast remains close to a 327.88 percent increase and the 2027 forecast is revised upward such that the decline is less than 25.82 percent, confidence in the medium-term earnings profile would likely improve, potentially supporting the share price.

Conversely, a reduction in the current-year expectation combined with a deeper projected drop in 2027 earnings would highlight downside risk, and the market could respond by moving the stock away from the EUR 13.07 reference point in either direction depending on broader sentiment.

Analyst consensus is only one piece of the puzzle, but the quantified comparison between the strong rebound in 2026 and the thereafter expected decline in 2027 gives a concrete framework that investors can use alongside their own assessment of the company’s strategy and the renewable fuels market.

This framework can also be compared with other energy transition players, where some firms show smoother earnings trajectories but potentially lower near-term growth, while others share Neste’s pattern of sharp recoveries from weak periods followed by normalization.

Neste’s renewable products as a core driver

A central part of Neste’s business model is the production of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuels, which are designed to reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared with traditional fossil-based fuels while leveraging existing infrastructure.

Within this portfolio, the company’s renewable diesel products are a key contributor to both revenue and margins, as they allow customers in transportation and logistics to achieve emission reduction targets without fully shifting to electric or hydrogen-based solutions.

Demand for such renewable fuels has been supported by regulatory frameworks in Europe and North America, where blending mandates and incentives encourage the use of lower-emission alternatives in road transport and aviation.

Over the medium term, uptake of sustainable aviation fuel is expected to grow as airlines and airports commit to decarbonization pathways, with several carriers announcing plans to increase the share of sustainable aviation fuel in their total fuel mix through the late 2020s.

For Neste, each incremental increase in sustainable aviation fuel demand can translate into additional volumes sold, helping to support the earnings rebound seen in current-year forecasts and potentially influencing the trajectory of future-year expectations as capacity is ramped up.

The company’s investment program in new renewable production capacity and supply chains is therefore a critical element in determining whether the projected 327.88 percent earnings increase for 2026 is a one-off recovery or part of a broader transition to structurally higher profitability.

If ongoing projects come online within budget and on schedule, they may help mitigate the forecasted 25.82 percent decline in 2027 earnings by adding new sources of margin and volume that offset normalization effects in existing operations.

However, delays or cost overruns in these projects could exacerbate the expected earnings volatility, making the consensus pattern of a sharp rebound followed by a decline more pronounced in realized numbers.

Current stock level and investor takeaway

With Neste stock trading around EUR 13.07 on the Helsinki exchange as of August 28, 2026, the current market level reflects a balance between the aggressive earnings rebound forecast for the present year and the modeled pullback in 2027.

For retail investors, the key figures to keep in view are the share price reference of EUR 13.07, the 327.88 percent expected increase in current-year earnings and the 25.82 percent projected decline for next year, which together define a story of strong recovery followed by normalization rather than uninterrupted growth.

As quarterly results and updated guidance are released over the coming months, changes in these consensus metrics and the share price relative to EUR 13.07 will provide ongoing signals about how the market is reassessing the company’s earnings power and valuation.

text:
The Nationals leader Matt Canavan and Shadow Minister for Infrastructure and Transport, Bridget McKenzie were in Perth over the weekend for the Nationals WA state conference. Picture by Tamara Hooper.

Western Australians are staring down the barrel of rising fuel costs under the Low Carbon Liquid Fuels (LCLF) industry, a part of the Future Made in Australia plan the Federal government is fast tracking.

The domestic LCLF industry will initially focus on sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel to reduce emissions in fuel reliant sectors, including agriculture, transport (aviation, heavy vehicle, rail and maritime), construction and mining.

The government also committed $1.5 million over two years from 2024-25 to undertake a regulatory impact analysis of the costs and benefits of introducing mandates or other demand-side measures for LCLF.

While critics and opposition figures argue the system functions as a hidden tax that will drive up retail fuel prices and airfares, the Federal government has not yet confirmed exact commencement dates, mandatory blending percentages, or finalised cost impacts on end-users while consultation remains ongoing.

Rural transporters and farmers will be the hardest hit by any added costs related to fuel which would be in addition to the Heavy Vehicle Road Users Charge (RUC) and Fuel Excise Duty Rates.

Driven by Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, the Federal government released a consultation paper exploring a tradeable carbon-credit and volume-based blending target system.

Mr Bowen said Australia could not afford to be vulnerable to fuel supply disruptions beyond its shores.

"That's why we're making a historic investment to strengthen fuel security, support domestic refining and build the cleaner fuels industries of the future," Mr Bowen said.

"We're strengthening Australia's resilience by building larger fuel reserves, increasing stockholdings and backing domestic industry to produce more of the fuels we need here at home.

"By strengthening fuel security today and building cleaner fuel industries for tomorrow, we're delivering practical economic and environmental benefits for Australian households, businesses and communities."

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, and Shadow Minister for Infrastructure and Transport, Bridget McKenzie, were in Perth over the weekend, for The Nationals WA State conference and labelled Labor's LCLF measures an "extension of the Net Zero, a carbon tax on fuel".

Mr Canavan said Labor's consultation paper on securing liquid fuels points towards a new fuel carbon tax as the 'most favourable' new tax.

"Chris Bowen's answer to our fuel crisis is to resuscitate a Labor carbon tax on fuels, devastating families and businesses who are already struggling under Labor's cost of living crisis," he said.

"As Labor's own consultation paper states, costs will be imposed on trade-exposed sectors, regional and remote communities."

He said the report, Securing Australia's Cleaner Fuels Industry: Consultation paper on a demand mechanism, suggests that importing more fuel, rather than looking at Australian production pathways, could be more 'cost-competitive', depending on future import prices.

Nationals WA leader Shane Love discussed support for the biofuel manufacturing industry, which is another arm of ensuring Australia's sovereign capacity to provideits own fuel. Picture by Tamara Hooper.

"Labor's net zero scam is not a transition - it is a transfer of wealth from Australian families and a transfer of jobs from our country to overseas," Mr Canavan said.

"Labor's answer to our fuel crisis is not just more tax on our petrol for Australian families and businesses, but also a forced reliance on other nations for our fuel security.

"Labor would rather tax families extra for petrol and go begging, cap in hand, to other countries for fuel, instead of relying on our own resources and creating our own fuel security.

"This means more industries closing, more jobs and manufacturing offshore, and an enormous burden all along our food supply chain.

"Families are already struggling with escalating power bills, lack of housing supply and our living standards going backwards, but instead of Labor admitting its net zero plan has failed, it is doubling down and forcing its disastrous agenda onto all Australians, which will just make everyone poorer and life even harder.

"I think anybody that said net zero policy was going to mean net zero cost, is learning the folly of that statement. "

Shadow Minister for Infrastructure and Transport, Bridget McKenzie, said Labor's proposed new carbon tax and credits trading scheme would further punish Australians who drive petrol and diesel vehicles, targeting those who cannot afford to buy a new taxpayer subsidised EV.

"The Coalition has consistently supported an all technologies approach to lowering transport emissions, including biofuels, which have a role to play in enhancing fuel security and supporting Australian industries," Ms McKenzie said.

"Now Labor wants to hit motorists with yet another tax each time they fill up.

"The government's own document makes it very clear who will pay for this new carbon tax on fuel, and that is the end consumer."

Ms McKenzie said the government needs to come clean on the higher costs its hidden modelling shows this new fuel tax would impose on the community.

Minister for Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government, Catherine King, said Labor was investing in the fuels the aviation, maritime and freight industries needed.

"Currently, we export up to $6 billion of feedstocks each year, including canola and tallow, for global markets," Ms King said.

"By building a low carbon liquid fuels industry right here, we will create more jobs, build regional economies, strengthen our fuel security and future-proof our transport industries."

Shadow Minister for Energy and Emissions Reduction Dan Tehan said that you don't boost Australia's fuel security by introducing new taxes.

"Yet that's exactly what Labor is setting up to do, with their so-called carbon-intensity standard - which is just a fancy name for a massive new carbon tax," Mr Tehan said.

"Labor's spending is out of control; they have just hit $1 trillion in debt and now they want to make fuel more expensive.

"Only Chris Bowen would think this makes sense.

"The consultation paper specifically says that it is "not possible" to figure out by how much emissions would be reduced where there is an overlap between Labor's new fuel tax and the Safeguard Mechanism.

"So Labor is setting up a new carbon tax but can't even say by how much emissions would be reduced, which is their primary aim."

GrainGrowers, in their submission, stated Australia was already a major supplier of canola to the European Union biodiesel market, exporting over 1.8 million tonnes annually.

Ms McKenzie said the National Party has always been the political movement that backs small to medium enterprises.

PGA of WA president Digby Stretch said any added cost to fuel was gojng to add further harm to regional WA. Picture by Tamara Hooper.

"We back competition laws, that means you can thrive," Ms McKenzie said.

We don't want to see WA or indeed Australia, only have large monopoly players in any industry.

"We will always be backing the independent distributive network, our road transport industry, the small to medium enterprises with one to 15 trucks on the books, doing everything they can, to get the grain in and the livestock where it needs to be.

"We've seen repeated mistakes out of Canberra that have seen the cash flow of these transport businesses under pressure."

She said this was a situation the Nationals were being very careful to avoid.

"We have been calling for the Albanese government to provide fuel exercise relief and make sure that the transport operators aren't having to make up the difference," she said.

"In terms of fuel security, we've been very, very clear that we support more biofuels into the fuel supply chain.

"As long as it doesn't drive up price at the bowser, because we see that as a win, not just for fuel security, but, indeed, for our primary producers, in having a diversity of markets.

"It's appalling that we send grain overseas to be processed, and used by others, in a lower emissions future."

Leader of The Nationals WA, Shane Love said when the Strait of Hormuz became an issue, farmers were desperate to get fuel, and there were no systems in place to ensure that.

"So we've got to make sure that we don't ever see a repeat of that shortage," Mr Love said.

"Australia has roughly a month or so of fuel, that's not a lot when you don't have your own solid capacity to provide fuel.

"At the moment, much of Western Australia's canola crop is exported to Europe to be converted into fuel.

"We will be discussing support for the biofuel industry manufacturing industry, which is another arm of ensuring we have the sovereign capacity to provide our own fuel."

We are a dead exporter of energy, if you like, with the gas and the compensates, which can be sent overseas, or sent to the Eastern States for processing.

"We could do much, much more to ensure we have our own fuel capacity, our own fuel sovereignty in the future."

On July 1, the RUC reverted from the relief figure of 16.4c/L, up to 32.4c/L, with it scheduled to increase further to 34.3c/L from January 1.

ALRTA executive director Ben Maguire said there were few viable alternatives to diesel for rural transporters. Picture by Tamara Hooper.

"The volume of fuel used in the regions, by people who have to travel those long distances, highlights a completely unfair tax on people in the country.

"When you see your problem, and you raise a new tax - no, that's not a solution, that's just a new problem you brought to the whole system."

Australian Livestock & Rural Transporters Association (ALRTA) executive director Ben Maguire said livestock and rural operators already carry a heavy burden, with few practical alternatives to diesel available.

"At a time of heightened geopolitical uncertainty, governments should be strengthening the resilience of our supply chains, not imposing further costs that make them more fragile," Mr Maguire said.

"The ALRTA will work through the consultation process with our members, the Australian Trucking Association and other peak bodies to understand the details and prepare a response."

Livestock and Rural Transport Association of WA president, Ben Sutherland, said it would be just forcing another tax on transporters.

"It is yet another small business hindrance," Mr Sutherland said.

"They have indexed the fuel excise and then plan on raising the heavy vehicle road users up again in January.

"How much more can they expect us to take and survive as small business operators?"

title: India's sustainable aviation fuel can achieve cost parity with jet fuel by 2036: Report
description:

The report by Gulf Times said that evaluating SAF projects only through single-year production costs gives an incomplete picture of their long-term economics.
In addition, historical data between 2005 and 2025 showed wholesale jet fuel prices rising by 5 per cent annually in nominal rupee terms.
Under base-case market assumptions, new synthetic fuel facilities commissioned in 2036 are projected to achieve full levelised cost parity with conventional fuel, the report said.
These benefits could potentially bring SAF to commercial cost parity with conventional jet fuel as early as 2030, it said.

New Delhi: India's sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) industry could achieve cost parity with conventional jet fuel by 2036 with domestic production offering greater protection from currency fluctuations and global commodity price volatility, a report has said.

The report by Gulf Times said that evaluating SAF projects only through single-year production costs gives an incomplete picture of their long-term economics.

It noted that while power-and-biomass-to-liquids (PBtL) fuel is estimated to cost $1.42 per litre in 2030, compared with $0.97 per litre for conventional jet fuel, the gap narrows substantially when costs are assessed over a 25-year project cycle.

In addition, historical data between 2005 and 2025 showed wholesale jet fuel prices rising by 5 per cent annually in nominal rupee terms.

About 1.9 per cent of the increase was attributed to US dollar commodity inflation, while 3.1 per cent reflected rupee depreciation against the dollar.

According to the report, domestic synthetic fuel plants can help reduce this currency vulnerability as major operational inputs can be secured through long-term, rupee-denominated power purchase agreements at fixed tariffs.

Taking these dynamics into account, researchers estimated the levelised cost of PBtL fuel from a plant commissioned in 2030 at Rs 127 per litre, only 18 per cent above the adjusted levelised purchase cost of conventional jet fuel over the same 25-year period.

Under base-case market assumptions, new synthetic fuel facilities commissioned in 2036 are projected to achieve full levelised cost parity with conventional fuel, the report said.

It also noted that the cost gap could close sooner if the wider economic benefits of green fuel are factored into policy decisions.

Moreover, monetising health benefits from reduced agricultural field burning could add an estimated $0.38 per litre in avoided societal costs, while applying carbon costs could add up to $0.22 per litre.

These benefits could potentially bring SAF to commercial cost parity with conventional jet fuel as early as 2030, it said.

Additionally, the report highlighted the potential for India's agricultural residue and low-cost renewable power to support a domestic SAF ecosystem while reducing exposure to imported crude oil and foreign exchange risks.

title: Who Gets Paid for Cleaner Aviation Fuel? - Zenith Net-Zero
description:
